This vector was used in Fig. 2 to label all RGCs and examine their neuronal output in SC.

AAV2-CAG-DIO-mWGA-mCherry (DIO-mWmC, Addgene ID 263584) was produced as AAV Serotype 2 (Virovek, catalogue no. 117-UCSF86, at 4 × 1013 vg ml−1) following Tsai et al.6 and produced at Virovek using BAC-to-AAV technology. This vector was used in Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6 to label specific types of RGCs and analyse their output in SC.

According to recent reports, AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE (Addgene ID 100054) (Serotype 2 produced at Boston Children’s Hospital Viral Core, at 2× 1013 vg ml−1) was used in Fig. 2 for CRACM experiments from all RGCs to examine their connectivity onto SC neurons.

Sources indicate that AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry (Addgene ID 20297) (Serotype 2 produced at UNC Viral Core, at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1) was used in Fig. 3 for CRACM experiments in Cartpt-cre mice to assess connectivity with SC neurons in the RFP channel.

AAV2-EF1α-FDIO-GFP-WPRE (Addgene ID 203843) was used to label SC neurons in Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines in the GFP channel.

AAV8-EF1α-FDIO-GCaMP6s (Addgene ID 105714) was used to label SC neurons in Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines for in vivo calcium imaging.

AAV2-Flex-taCasp3-TEVp (Addgene ID 45580) (Serotype 2 produced at UNC Viral Core, at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1)62 was used to selectively ablate retinal SACs in ChAT-Cre mice.

AAV8-hSyn-FRT-TVA-P2A-EGFP-2A-oG63 was modified and produced by X.C., as Serotype 8, at 2× 1013 vg ml−1, which enabled efficient, FlpO-dependent retrograde tracing in restricted neuronal subsets, including Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO SC neurons, as shown in Fig. 3.

According to recent reports, envA G-deleted Rabies–mCherry (Addgene ID 32636) was obtained from the Salk GT3 Core (catalogue no. 32636). Used in combination with TVA-2A-oG, it enabled retrograde labelling of presynaptic retinal neurons of defined SC starter populations in Fig. 3.

Sources indicate that AAV2-CAG-membrane bound YFP (AAV-CAG-mYFP, Addgene ID 263585) was modified from AAV-EF1a-BbTagBY (Addgene ID 45185)64. AAV serotype 2 was produced at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1 and used for projection axon labelling65. Following intraocular injection, it enabled visualization of axonal projections in SC.

AAV2-CAG-DIO-membrane bound YFP (AAV-CAG-DIO-mYFP, Addgene ID 263586) was modified from AAV-EF1a-BbTagBY (Addgene ID 45185). AAV serotype 2 was produced at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1 and used in combination with Cre-driver mouse lines to selectively label axons of defined RGC starter populations. This enabled visualization of cell-type-specific RGC axonal projections in SC.

According to recent reports, the brain preparation for TransA-MERFISH was optimized to preserve immunohistochemical staining and maximize RNA quality for subsequent RNA multiplexing experiments. Young adult mice were deeply anaesthetized and transcardially perfused with ice-cold saline (0.9% NaCl solution), followed by ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). After dissection, the brains were post-fixed in the same fixative solution overnight at 4 °C. The target brain regions (SC in this study, about 10 mm3 in volume) were micro-dissected, with anteroposterior and dorsoventral orientations carefully marked. This was followed by cryoprotection in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissues sank (2–4 h). The target regions were embedded in OCT compound and rapidly frozen in a dry ice-cooled 2-methylbutane (Supelco, MX0760-1). Then, approximately 12 µm coronal sections were prepared on a cryostat and collected under RNase-free conditions on MERSCOPE Slides (Vizgen) for RNA-grade processing.

Recent findings suggest that for each mouse, about 10 coronal sections were obtained using the right SC, which receives contralateral retinal input from the left eye injected with mWmC tracer, from the perfusion–fixation protocol described above. Sections were collected at intervals of every 9 slices (12 µm each, totalling about 100 µm), spanning the anterior-to-posterior axis of the right SC. The coronal sections encompassing the SC were selected based on the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, corresponding to stereotaxic coordinates relative to Bregma ranging from −3.0 mm to −5.0 mm. The section captures the full dorsoventral extent of the SC, from the superficial visual layers stratum zonale (SZ), SGS, to deep motor-associated layers stratum griseum profundum (SGP) and stratum album profundum (SAP).

The SC tissues on MERSLIDES (Vizgen, 20400001) were first permeablized in 70% ethanol (4°C) overnight, followed by a series of ethanol gradient dehydration: 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, 100% ethanol at room temperature for 1 h, 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, and then incubated with 70% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min. SC sections were then prepared for MERSCOPE imaging using the MERSCOPE Sample Preparation Kit (Vizgen, 10400012) and following the MERSCOPE User Guide (Fresh and Fixed Frozen Tissue Sample Preparation, 91600002 RevF).

For protein staining, the sample was washed with 5 ml of PBS. Blocking solution (10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor) (Blocking Buffer C, Vizgen 20300100; RNase inhibitor Murine, NEB M0314L) was then added to the centre of the tissue section and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. The sample was incubated in Primary Staining Solution (100:10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor: Primary antibody) at room temperature for 1 h. Notably, anti-RFP (rabbit, Rockland 46510) was diluted 1:100 for this step. The sample was subsequently washed with PBS. Secondary Staining Solution (100:10:3:1 Blocking Buffer Premix: RNase inhibitor: Secondary Stain Mix : Protein Stain) (Anti-Rabbit Protein Stain Kit, Vizgen, 10400107) was then added to the sample and incubated for 1 h. The sample was then washed with PBS. Fixation Buffer (4% PFA in PBS) was then added to the tissue section, and the section was incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The sample was then washed with PBS.

Next, for encoding probe hybridization, the sample was incubated in 5 ml Formamide Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300002) at 37 °C for 30 min. The Formamide Wash Buffer was then carefully aspirated, and the custom 140-Gene MERSCOPE Gene Panel Mix (Vizgen, VZG180, mouse superficial SC panel; Supplementary Table 1) was added to the tissue section, which was then incubated in a humidified chamber at 37 °C for at least 36 h and up to 48 h. Then, in the post-encoding probe hybridization washes, Formamide Wash Buffer was added to the sample and incubated at 47 °C for 30 min. This wash step was repeated, then the sample was incubated in the Sample Prep Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300001) for 2 min.

Recent findings suggest that then for gel embedding, wash buffer was aspirated from the MERSLIDE, and Gel Embedding Solution (2:10:1 Gel Embedding Premix: 10% w/v ammonium persulfate solution: N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine) (Gel Embedding Premix, Vizgen 20300004; ammonium persulfate, Sigma-Aldrich 09913; N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine, Sigma-Aldrich T7024) was added to cover the tissue sections. A coverslip pretreated with Gel Slick (VWR, 12001-812) was placed directly over the tissue sections and incubated at room temperature for 90 min to allow the gel to solidify. The coverslip was then removed. Then, the sample was treated to clear it. The sample was incubated in a pre-warmed Clearing Solution (100:1 Clearing Premix: Proteinase K) (Clearing Premix, Vizgen 20300003; Proteinase K, NEB P8107S) at 47 °C for 24 h.

For DAPI and PolyT staining, after removing the Clearing Solution, the sample was washed with a Sample Prep Wash Buffer. DAPI and PolyT Staining Reagent (Vizgen 20300021) were then added to the sample, which was incubated at room temperature for 15 min on a rocker. This was followed by a 10-min wash with Formamide Wash Buffer, then a 5 ml wash with 5 ml Sample Prep Buffer.

Finally, for MERFISH imaging, the sample was loaded onto the MERSCOPE instrument (MERSCOPE1.0, VIZGEN) for imaging, using the MERSCOPE 140 Gene Imaging Kit (Vizgen, 10400004), which automates the MERFISH probe exchange and readout.

Industry observers note that to design an SC-specific MERFISH gene panel, we first assessed the number of genes required to classify SC neuron types. To this end, we implemented a simulation framework based on gradient boosting (XGBoost) using SC single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data. In brief, for each neuron cluster, the top k non-redundant specific genes were selected to form a panel. The validation accuracy (using a 70:30 training:test split) was evaluated until a plateau was reached. Thus, after subsetting neuron cells from the adult SC snRNA-seq data28, we then re-clustered the cells using the Seurat standard log-normalization pipeline with the following functions: “NormalizeData” with default parameters, “FindVariableFeatures” (selection.method = ‘vst’), ScaleData (vars.to.regress =”nCount_RNA”), “RunPCA” (npcs=50), FindNeighbors (dims=1:35, dimension chosen by “ElbowPlot”), “FindClusters”, and “RunUMAP” (dim=35). The clusters were labelled based on the original cell-type labels, and 19 Leiden clusters recapitulating the original neuronal cell-type compartments were generated (Extended Data Fig. 2e). We then derived top marker genes for each type using the “FindAllMarkers” function with the “MAST” test (min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold=0.25, latent.vars = “nCount_RNA”).

To rank the marker genes, an integrated specificity score was calculated for each gene by retaining only those genes detected in over 40% of cells within the target cell type and calculating a log-ratio specificity score as:.

where pct.1 and pct.2 represent the proportion of expressing cells in the target and background populations, respectively, and ϵ = 0.02 is a pseudocount. To integrate both specificity and fold change, z-scores were independently computed for the log-ratio specificity score and the average log2-transformed fold change (avg_log2FC) within each cluster. The final Stouffer score was computed as:.

The hybrid score captures both binary specificity (expression prevalence) and quantitative magnitude (fold change), enabling robust ranking of marker genes per cluster.

In a recent development, we next selected the top k (k = 1 to 10) non-redundant, high-specificity marker genes for each neuronal subtype (a total of 19 types, as identified above). We used them as features to train an XGBoost classifier. To ensure comparability across genes, the normalized expression matrix was subset to the selected gene panel and scaled by centreing each gene to its mean and dividing by its standard deviation (z-score normalization across cells). The classifier was trained using a multi-class softmax objective (multi:softprob) over 200 boosting rounds, with a learning rate (η) of 0.2, maximum tree depth of 6, and subsampling rate of 0.6 to mitigate overfitting. The number of output classes was set to the number of unique neuronal subtypes. Training was performed on 70% of the cells (stratified by cluster), and performance was evaluated on the 30% held-out data. For each cell, the predicted label corresponded to the class with the highest probability. A confusion matrix comparing predicted and true labels demonstrated high concordance, confirming that the MERFISH panel accurately recovered neuronal subtype heterogeneity. Classification accuracy as a function of gene panel size was summarized in a line plot (Extended Data Fig. 1e), revealing a performance plateau at 0.8414 when k = 9 (171 genes), followed by a slight decline to 0.8403 at k = 10 (190 genes). Notably, despite the inclusion of additional top marker genes, this accuracy remained lower than that achieved with the MERFISH gene panel (0.91).

Among the 140 genes included in the panel, we selected markers enriched in pan-excitatory, pan-inhibitory and type-specific neuronal populations. The 140 genes include Ntng1, Meis1, Cpne4, Cacna2d1, Sgcd, Spon1, Kctd8, Gpc5, Ptprk, Nxph1, Robo1, Hs3st4, Sorcs3, Chrm3, Mgat4c, Syt1, Car10, Pcbp3, Reln, Trpm3, Meis2, Prkd1, Epha3, Fras1, Il1rapl2, Tmem132d, Fstl4, Erbb4, Ebf3, Ebf1, Maf, Ptprt, Cdh18, Npas3Htr2c, Tfap2b, Etv1, Tshz2, Sorcs1, Lhfp, Col25a1, Sox6, Adarb2, Megf11, Pde1c, Csgalnact1, Cdh8, Chrm2, Tcf7l2, Sphkap, Arpp21, Kirrel3, Zfhx3, Tmem132c, Hcn1 Hdac9, Rorb, Pdzd2, Adam12, Ankfn1, Sntb1, Npnt, Gpc3, Kcnd3, Tpd52l1, Myh8, Cdh7, Barhl1, Kcnab1, Rd3l, Cbln4, Otx2, Gabrr2, Cdhr1, Sox14, Dmbx1, Lhx1os, Galnt14, Tnnt1, Tnni3, Fibcd1, Mgarp, Lmo1, Vwc2, Npffr1, Rnf152, Zfhx4, Tal1, Trim66, Gata3, Syt2, Nrtn, Smim17, Pax7, Cdh13, Slc17a6, Tac1, Cbln2, Kcng3, Kcng4, Cdh4, Pde5a, Gda, Foxp2, Pou4f2, Sema3e, Gad2, Npas4, Sdk2, Ppia, Atp5md, Mllt11, Calb2, Nap1l5, Gap43, Tacr1, C1ql2, Fabp5, Cxcl14, Stmn1, Fos, Snap25, Junb, Pmfbp1, Ntng2, Pcdh20, Satb1, Sv2c, Fign, Gfra1, Syt17, Rasgrf2, Lmo3, Slc19a1, Cplx3, Marcksl1, Cadps2, Calb1, Syt4 and Gad1.

To further benchmark performance, we compared the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel against 2 control gene sets: (1) 140 genes randomly sampled from the full snRNA-seq expression matrix; and (2) 140 genes randomly sampled from the top 2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs). For each control set, we sampled genes without replacement and repeated the process 15 times to estimate variability (error bars) in classification accuracy. Using the same classification framework, our panel consistently outperformed both controls and the marker gene approach described above (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Two genes among the 140-gene panel (Sgcd and Ppia) were excluded due to low transcript detection in the TransA-MERFISH SC dataset and poor specificity for SC neuronal types.

Recent findings suggest that for each 12 µm tissue section, the MERFISH protocol generated seven 1.7 µm optical sections (z0, z1, … , z6) for DAPI, polyT and mCherry/RFP channels, respectively, as Tiff files under the images folder, together with the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv to link the micrometre scale (transcripts and MERSCOPE visualizer) to mosaic pixel scale (Tiff files). Each MERFISH data folder also contains the detected_transcripts.csv file, which includes coordinates for detected transcripts along with their spatial coordinates, as well as other metadata and cell-by-gene information. Cell segmentation information is also generated by the Vizgen Post-processing Tool (VPT). To improve cell segmentation accuracy, we performed independent segmentation using custom scripts and a fine-tuned Cellpose2.0 model tailored to the SC, as described below.

According to recent reports, the following steps were conducted: (1) DAPI image preprocessing and initial region-of-interest (ROI) selection. The DAPI image of z-plane 0 for each region is loaded into a Python Jupyter notebook (tifffile.imread), and overexposed pixels are filtered using a cut-off at the 0.95 quantile (np.quantile) to enhance the signal for downstream ROI selection. For each region, the initial ROI was restricted to the right SC hemisphere as our AAV2-mWmC injection was onto the left eye (Fig. 1a) and manually delineated using the processed DAPI image in ImageJ (Analyze-Tools-ROI manager), from the pial surface to encompass superficial SC layers (SZ and SGS) medially toward the midline, extending ventrally to the level of the cerebral aqueduct. This ROI includes both superficial and deeper layers as defined by cytoarchitectonic boundaries in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. We then cropped the original DAPI Tiff images of each seven z-plane images of one section to the delineated ROI (using the read_roi function, the matplotlib.patches module’s Polygon class, and the PIL package’s Image module). A maximum z-projection approach was performed over optical sections to enhance cell segmentation signals. To this end, the maximum-intensity projection of all seven z-plane optical sections for each slice was generated using either ImageJ (Images-Stack-Z Project) or Python (numpy.max). Meanwhile, we subset the detected_transcripts.csv file from MERFISH to correspond to the selected ROI (read-roi to load ImageJ ROI file, followed by matplotlib.path.Path in Python), using the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv file to transform transcript coordinates (global_x and global_y coordinates) to the mosaic pixel coordinates of the Tiff images, along with gene symbols for each detected transcript.

It has been revealed that segmentation was performed as in previous MERFISH studies of the mouse brain31. We constructed a labelled image by combining the transcript dots and maximum-intensity projection DAPI images using the get_img function (windowsize=2000, margin=10%) of the ClusterMap package, followed by splitting the data into small tiles (split function) to improve downstream computational efficiency. We set a threshold of 3,000 transcript counts to focus on tiles with denser transcript accumulation. The split tiles were then saved as separate PNG files with DAPI signal and transcript dots overlaid. A customized Cellpose model66 (models.CellposeModel pretrained_model) was used to perform cell segmentation on each tile (gpu=True, channels = [0,0], diameter=80). More specifically, the fine-tuned Cellpose model was generated based on the ‘cyto2’ model using the Cellpose graphical user interface, trained with five regions of interest (containing about 200 manually curated cells each), to improve the performance for dimly/darkly stained cells, smaller cells, and separating multiple cells that were segmented as one. The segmentation output for each tile was subsequently generated using the masks_flows_to_seg function from cellpose.io and saved as a.npy file. The separate tiles were then stitched by merging adjacent patches, while avoiding cell ID collisions and duplication in overlapping regions, to form the full segmentation mask (reassigned_masks.npy), which encompassed the entire tissue section. After all tiles were stitched, connected components in the combined mask were relabelled (skimage.measure.label and regionprops) to ensure sequential, non-overlapping cell IDs. We then assembled the AnnData for downstream analysis by constructing a ClusterMap model for each section, using the transcriptomic spot information (xy_radius=30, z_radius=0, fast_preprocess=False). Centroid positions were calculated from labelled masks using skimage.regionprops, and used to initialize cell-centred AnnData objects. Cells with no transcriptomic counts were excluded by default, and spatial coordinates were stored in the obsm[‘spatial’] field of the AnnData object. We further double-checked the accuracy of the assembled AnnData by comparing the transcript distribution and the segmentation of a specific cell to the combined raw data for DAPI, PolyT, and transcript dots from the same cell in the MERSCOPE visualizer. We then integrated the mean mCherry fluorescence intensity, mWmC registration-related metadata, and the estimated depth (in µm; distance from the pial surface, as described below) into a unified AnnData object.

According to recent reports, last, related to the entire TransA-MERFISH data integration, for consistency with the ROI of other data modalities, such as electrophysiology and calcium imaging, we also further restricted the above-selected ROI to rectangular regions, avoiding the midlines and lateral regions, encompassing from the pial surface to SO by examining the spatial expression of Npnt and Etv1 (Fig. 1j). Subsequent clustering and transcriptomic analyses of the resulting cell-by-gene matrix were performed using Scanpy (v1.10.4) and Squidpy (v1.6.2), as detailed in the following sections.

In a recent development, to register mWmC+ cells in the TransA-MERFISH dataset, we implemented an automated registration workflow based on per-cell mCherry intensity, supplemented by manual curation. First, we derive the per-cell mean mCherry intensity by aggregating the mean mCherry pixel intensity at each z-layer (z = 1:6, excluding z0 to avoid potential optical noise). The aggregated value was then divided by the number of z-planes (six in this case, as the maximum-intensity projection-derived cell segmentation mask was shared across z-planes), yielding a per-cell mean mCherry intensity across z-planes. The frequency distribution of the per-cell mean mCherry intensity highlighted a predominantly bimodal distribution of red fluorescence. Second, we assigned an mWmC-positive score using the mean intensity value from the inner cytoplasm ring area and an adjacent out-of-cell annulus as a local background estimate. The positive cells were identified by applying a threshold based on the distributions from a control ROI (in the lower, non-retino-recipient area with the lowest red fluorescence signal) on the same slice. Last, mWmC+ cells were proofread by two independent annotators for all slices, who examined the red fluorescence overlaid on the DAPI and PolyT labelling, with or without segmented cell masks, using Vizgen MERSCOPE Visualizer. The Python script for the workflow was deposited on GitHub (https://github.com/duanxlab/TransA-MERFISH).

For the background-corrected per-cell quantification of mCherry fluorescence, we implemented an integrated workflow for image denoising, fluorescence background removal, per-cell mWmC score calculation, and threshold assignment following the steps below.

First, background correction: to remove uneven illumination and background fluorescence (especially signals in axons, which reside in the same lamina as the recipient neurons), we applied a multi-threaded rolling-ball background subtraction algorithm to the RFP channel image. For each section, the maximum-intensity projection of z0–z7 optical planes was used as input. The image was processed in overlapping tiles (4,096 × 4,096 pixels) with a rolling-ball radius of 80 pixels. For each tile, the background surface was computed using the skimage.restoration.rolling_ball function, and the results were then merged across tiles to form a continuous background field. The corrected image was obtained by subtracting this field from the raw mosaic and clipping negative values to zero. The resulting background-subtracted image was used for downstream analyses. After this correction, the background intensity was reduced to baseline, thereby removing the haze surrounding individual cells. By contrast, the pixel intensity within cell masks is largely preserved. Second, further background removal and per-cell signal quantification: following the above background correction by rolling ball, residual local background (for example, neuropils and axons) around each labelled soma was estimated and removed using a ring-based subtraction procedure. In brief, for each segmented soma (cell i), the soma mask was eroded by 1 pixel to define a core region and then dilated by a 4-pixel guard band to prevent the background annulus from abutting the soma edge. This guarded soma was then surrounded by a series of concentric annuli (inner width = 8 pixels; outer radius range = 12–30 pixels) from which background intensity was sampled. Background pixels were sampled from the annulus after excluding any pixels belonging to other cells. The local background level Bi was defined as the 25th percentile of annular intensities. The corrected image \({I}^{{\prime} }(x,y)\) was computed as,.

For every soma and the designated ring configuration, we reported pre- and post-subtraction statistics within the inner measurement region (soma-adjacent ring):.

along with background noise estimates from the annulus:.

Sources indicate that along with \({\sigma }_{\text{STD}}\) (sample standard deviation). After the removal of local background, the above-defined inner ring highlights an improved local signal-to-noise ratio, and mWmC puncta signals stand out more.

Recent findings suggest that third, to define an internal control region and identify mWmC-positive cells in each section, we implemented automated identification of the control region and quantification of mWmC+ cells. In this pipeline, we used an automated depth-aware sliding-window analysis. For each cell i, the locally background-corrected fluorescence intensity was summarized by the mean pixel intensity within the soma’s inner measurement ring after local background subtraction, as described above. Cell centroids were computed from the segmentation mask, and a sliding window of height 800 µm was moved along the pial-to-deep axis in 100-µm increments. Within each window w, we computed the cumulative fluorescence energy as \({S}_{w}=\sum _{i\in w}{I}_{i},\) where Ii is the per-cell fluorescence metric (post-subtraction inner ring mean intensity in this case). Windows with fewer than 15 cells were excluded. The resulting curve Sw versus depth was smoothed with a seven-point moving average, and the valley (minimum) among valid windows was selected as the centre of the control region, corresponding to the zone of lowest cumulative signal (background). From this valley, the control region was symmetrically expanded until at least 600 cells were included. The final control region was exported as a rectangular ROI spanning the full mediolateral width. For all cells within the control ROI, Ii were aggregated to estimate the control population mean (μctrl) and standard deviation (σctrl). We then defined mWmC+ cells using the below threshold: after trimming the top 2% of brightest cells to exclude outliers confounded by, for example, neighbouring overexposed pixels, thresholds for positive detection were defined as T5σ = μctrl + 5σctrl as the baseline to register mWmC+ cells.

Finally, with the per-cell mWmC information, we further assigned a cell type as mWmC+ (retino-recipient) by first deriving the mWmC+ cell profiles across different cell types using the methods described above. Encouragingly, automatically assigned mWmC+ cell profiles correlate strongly with manual annotations, indicating consistency across methods. To quantify enrichment of mWmC+ cells across neuronal subtypes, we computed an enrichment score for each tracing and cell type using the following steps. For each tracing × cell type, we constructed a 2 × 2 table of mWmC+ and mWmC− counts inside the cell type versus all other cells and applied a one-tailed Fisher’s exact test (alternative = “greater”). The odds ratio (OR) was computed as:.

It has been revealed that where a and b are the numbers of mWmC+ and mWmC− cells within the given subtype, and c and d are the corresponding counts outside that subtype. The effect size was visualized as log2(OR) (values < 0 clipped to 0). At the same time, statistical evidence was encoded by a point area proportional to −log10(P). Cell types with positive enrichment (log2(OR) > 0) were highlighted with a red outline (Fig. 2o). We assign a cell type as positive or connected under a specific tracing condition when the log2(OR) value is greater than 0 (enrichment). Based on the mWmC+ cell types assigned here, we summarized the mean mWmC+ cell proportion across animals (error bar: s.e.m.) as bar plots (Figs. 1k and 3c).

According to recent reports, the neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. To determine parameters better reflect internal data structure and cell-type granularity, we chose clustering parameters based on statistical assessment and established parameter selection tools. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. The parameter selections here allowed us to settle on a granularity of cell types that best represent the internal data structure in an unbiased way. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below. Subsequent comparisons to published SC atlas showed high consistency, for example, when compared to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain Atlas at supertype level, supporting the robustness of selected parameters and the resulting granularity of cell types.

To perform clustering and dimension reduction, we first applied SCTransform-based normalization67 to the expression matrix for each MERFISH section. This was enabled by accessing the SCTransform algorithm implemented in the R package via rpy2 from Python. Prior to normalization, raw counts were stored in adata.layers[‘raw_counts’]. A quality control filtering step was then applied to remove low-quality features, retaining genes detected in at least 5 cells (sc.pp.filter_genes) and cells with a total count of at least 5 (sc.pp.filter_cells). After filtering, the sparse matrices were explicitly sorted to ensure compatibility. Each AnnData object was converted to a Seurat object (as.Seurat()), and SCTransform was applied (do.correct.umi = FALSE). SCTransform models sequencing depth (library size/total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)) as a technical covariate during normalization. The full set of normalized gene expression values was extracted from the SCT assay’s scale.data slot and stored in adata.layers[‘normalized’], ensuring that any genes missing post-normalization were reintroduced as zero-filled vectors to retain consistency with the original feature set. The normalized matrix was then assigned to adata.X for downstream analysis. Raw counts were preserved in adata.raw, and standard quality control metrics (n_genes_by_counts, total_counts) were computed using the raw layer. Based on the quality control metrics, two sections with low quality and significantly lower counts were excluded from further analysis.

In a recent development, the AnnDatas of the remaining MERFISH slices were subsequently merged using scanpy (v1.10.4; abbreviated as sc onwards) with ad.concat (merge = ‘unique’, index_unique=None), yielding a combined dataset of 47,740 cells. Cell identifiers were made unique across slices, and principal component analysis was performed on the merged expression matrix (sc.tl.pca). The variance explained by each component was examined to guide dimensionality reduction (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). A neighbourhood graph was constructed using the top 15 principal components (n_pcs = 15) and 30 nearest neighbours (n_neighbors = 30) by sc.pp.neighbors. UMAP was then applied for two-dimensional embedding (sc.tl.umap). Unsupervised clustering was carried out using the Leiden algorithm with a resolution parameter of 0.8 (sc.tl.leiden). We examined the distribution of quality control metrics across the clusters. We found high consistency of n_genes_by_counts and total_counts across clusters except lower detection rate in one cluster (Extended Data Fig. 1h), which was identified as non-neuronal cells via the SC XGBoost classifier as described above (Extended Data Fig. 1i). To improve classification resolution, the non-neuronal cluster was excluded, yielding 46,277 high-quality transcriptomic profiles for neuronal cells. The neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below.

Industry observers note that to robustly identify the molecular identity of the above-identified MERFISH clusters, we took the following steps to classify the identified clusters and compare them to established SC atlases: first, we examined the gene expression pattern for a set of SC canonical marker genes (Fig. 1g) and the dendrogram between these clusters based on hierarchical clustering of averaged expression per cluster (sc.tl.dendrogram). Second, we aligned our MERFISH data to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain (CCN20230722) taxonomy30 using the MapMyCells tool suite from the Allen Institute. Third, we utilized the XGBoost classifier, as described above, to link the MERFISH data to our and other published SC scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq neuron-type atlases6,27,28, using the shared genes between the MERFISH panel and the snRNA-seq genes as features (Extended Data Fig. 2c,g,j). Finally, we compared the expression pattern of key marker genes between our data and previously published SC datasets (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, the identified clusters captured the neuronal diversity of the SC at high resolution, demonstrating strong concordance—and in some cases, enhanced granularity—compared to established reference atlases.

We implemented a sublaminar-controlled cell-type specificity analysis to test the specificity of each SC type in specifying the connections with presynaptic RGC inputs (Fig. 2d). The analysis is based on a permutation-based statistical framework with Stouffer z-score aggregation across mice. More specifically, to assess cell-type–specific enrichment or depletion of mWmC+ labelling independent of sublaminar distribution, we performed a sublaminar-controlled permutation test. Within each mouse, SC neurons were binned by soma depth (50 µm unless otherwise specified). Within each (animal × depth bin) stratum, cell-type labels were randomly shuffled, thereby preserving the sublaminar distribution of mWmC labelling while disrupting the association between cell-type identity and mWmC labelling. All permutation tests were performed with 1,000 permutations using a fixed random seed unless otherwise stated. For each permutation, we computed the number of mWmC+ cells per cell type, yielding a null distribution of expected counts under the hypothesis that sublaminar position alone explains connectivity. Observed mWmC+ cell counts were then converted into per-animal z-scores relative to this null distribution. Specifically, for each cell type t and mouse q, the z-score was computed as follows,.

where \({N}_{t,q}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes the observed number of mWmC+ cells of type t in mouse q, and μt,q and σt,q denote the mean and standard deviation of the permutation-derived null distribution for that cell type and mouse. z-Scores provide a signed, normalized measure of enrichment or depletion relative to sublaminar expectation. z-Scores were then aggregated across mice using Stouffer’s method as below,.

where n is the number of mice. To test for bidirectional deviations (enrichment or depletion) of mWmC labelling beyond sublaminar expectation, two-sided P values were computed from the combined z-scores using the standard normal distribution as,.

In a recent development, and controlled for multiple comparisons across cell types using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Positive z-scores indicate enrichment beyond sublaminar expectation, whereas negative z-scores indicate depletion, reflecting cases in which sublaminar position alone overestimates the likelihood of receiving retinal input. As statistical inference is performed using normal-theory P values derived from the aggregated z-scores (after estimating null mean and variance from permutations), the minimum attainable P value is not constrained by the number of permutations. Finally, SC neuron types were ranked by their aggregated Stouffer z-scores, which we refer to as the cell-type specificity score, representing the preference of a cell type’s molecular identity for RGC connectivity (Fig. 2e).

RGC axons in the SC from four different genotypes and all RGCs were included. In brief, coronal brain sections were immunostained and imaged using a confocal microscope, as previously described43. Confocal stacks of 20 µm thickness were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Using ImageJ, each right SC hemisphere was divided into five equal sections. The fluorescence profile of axon arbors was measured by taking 200-μm-thick line scans perpendicular to each section’s pial surface, extending to a depth of 500 μm below it. Signal intensity values were normalized to the maximum intensity across images and plotted. The locally weighted scatterplot smoothing function in MATLAB was used to smooth the curve. ImageJ was used to analyse confocal stacks and produce maximum-intensity projections. To quantify axon depth across the SC, the shortest distance from the pial surface to the upper and lower boundaries of the axonal arbors was measured within each section. Five mice of each genotype, including all SC slices, were used for each experimental condition. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit/random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

Recent findings suggest that the retina histology protocol was described as previously described50. Mice were euthanized, and eyes were collected, then fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 1 h on ice. Retinas were dissected and rinsed with PBS. For the whole-mount retina data in Fig. 3, we adapted previously described protocols37. Whole-mount retina samples were blocked in blocking buffer (5% normal donkey serum, 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS) at room temperature for 1 h, then incubated with primary antibodies for 2–4 days at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. For mounting, retinas were placed flat, ganglion cell side up, and sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For retinal vertical sections in Extended Data Fig. 6, we adapted protocols previously described37. Fixed mouse retinas were cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS for 1 h before embedding in OCT (Epredia). Vertical retinal cryosections (20 µm) were prepared and mounted on glass slides. Sections were blocked in the same blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

According to recent reports, brain section histology was described previously68. Mice were deeply anaesthetized and perfused transcardially with ice-cold PBS, followed by 4% PFA. Brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissue blocks sank. Tissue was frozen directly on the stage of a sliding microtome (Leica) cooled with dry ice and sectioned coronally at 40 µm. Free-floating sections were blocked in the blocking buffer described above and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, then for 1 h at room temperature with secondary antibodies. Sections were mounted on slides with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

In a recent development, antibodies used were as follows: goat and chicken anti-GFP (1:1,000, Rockland; 1:500, Abcam); rabbit anti-RFP (1:1,000, Rockland for immunohistochemistry); mouse anti-SATB1 (marker for ooDSGC in reference69, 1:1,000, Santa Cruz); goat anti-choline acetyltransferase (ChAT, 1:500, Millipore); rabbit anti-CARTPT (1:2,500, Phoenix Pharmaceuticals); rabbit anti-TUSC5 (1:500, Novus); Rabbit anti-RBPMS (1:1,000, Poteintech/Fisher); goat anti-SPP1 (1:500, R&D); sheep anti-FOXP2 (1:500, R&D); rabbit anti-ETV1 (1:1,000, J.A.K.)70. Secondary antibodies were conjugated to Alexa Fluor 488, Alexa Fluor 568, or Alexa Fluor 647 (Jackson ImmunoResearch) and used at 1:1,000.

According to recent reports, in situ hybridization was performed as previously described68 using RNAscope Fluorescent Multiplex Kit (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, sections were fixed in 4% PFA and dehydrated as described in ‘Immunohistochemistry for the retina and SC’, followed by air drying. A hydrophobic barrier was drawn around the sections with an ImmEdge pen (Vector Labs, H-4000). The sections were post-fixed with 4% PFA, quenched with hydrogen peroxide, and subjected to target retrieval followed by dehydration in 100% ethanol. Sections were treated with Protease III, incubated with target probes, treated with a series of amplification reagents, and developed with TSA fluorophores. Slides were mounted using mounting medium (VECTASHIELD, Vector Laboratories). RNAscope probes included the following: Cdh7 (ACD #521331), Cbln4 (ACD #505411), Itga7 (ACD #542911) and Sntb1 (ACD #440541).

According to recent reports, intraocular injection of AAVs was performed as previously described37,41. Approximately 0.5 µl of virus was delivered into the left eye using a sharpened glass micropipette. All AAVs (serotype 2 targeting RGCs) were standardized to the same titre of 2 × 1013 genome copies. Mice were euthanized, and retinas and brains were collected about 4 weeks post-injection (wpi).

Sources indicate that for mWmC-based anterograde tracing experiments, AAV encoding constitutive mWmC or Cre-dependent mWmC was intravitreally injected into wild-type, Kcng4-cre, Cartpt-cre, Foxp2-cre and Tusc5-cre mice. AAVs were injected into the left eyes using a sharpened glass pipette as previously described19. Mice were processed for analysis at 4 wpi.

For optogenetic experiments, AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry were injected into the left eyes of mice to activate all RGCs or ooDSGCs. Mice were allowed to mature for at least 6 wpi, reaching adulthood (6–10 weeks) before analysis.

It has been revealed that for starburst amacrine cell (Chat+) ablation experiments, AAV2-Flex-taCasp3-TEVp was injected into the left eye or both eyes of mice in the ablation groups. 2 sites located at the dorsal and ventral parts of the eyeball were used for injection; 0.75 µl of virus was injected into each site. For the control groups, same volume of saline was injected into the left eye of mice. Two-photon calcium imaging was performed 1 month after injection.

According to recent reports, for adult SC labelling, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane during the surgery (3% for induction and 1.5–2% for maintenance) and placed in a stereotaxic apparatus (Model 940, David Kopf Instruments). Meloxicam (5 mg kg−1) was administered intraperitoneally for analgesia before the surgery and 1 day after the surgery. Body temperature was maintained at 37 °C using a homeothermic blanket. Viral solutions were loaded into a pulled glass pipette connected to a syringe (7634-0, Hamilton) via a dual-ferrule adaptor (55750-0, Hamilton). The injection speed and volume were controlled by a Microinjection Syringe Pump (UMP3T-1, WPI). AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-mCherry or AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-EGFP (1 µl) was injected into the right SC of adult mice at a constant speed (60 nl min−1).

Recent findings suggest that two injection sites were used for the Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines: one at 0.35 mm posterior and 0.5 mm lateral to lambda at a depth of 1.3 mm, and the other at 0.1 mm posterior and 0.6 mm lateral to lambda at a depth of 1.2 mm. The mice were transcardially perfused at 4 wpi. The brains were collected for immunohistochemical analysis. In addition, specifically for pseudorabies-mediated retrograde tracing, AAV8-hSyn-FRT-TVA-P2A-EGFP-2A-oG viruses (1 µl) were injected into the right SC of the Cdh7-FlpO or Cbln4-FlpO adult mice by stereotaxic injections as described above. Three weeks later, EnvA G-Deleted Rabies-mCherry (1.2 µl) was injected into the right SC. Six days post-rabies injection, mice were transcardially perfused, and brains and contralateral (left) retinas were collected for immunohistochemical analysis.

Sources indicate that we used the Cre/FlpO strategy to label SC neurons and manipulate RGCs separately by crossing RGC-specific Cre drivers to SC-specific FlpO mice. After injecting AAV2-EF1α-FDIO-GFP-WPRE into the right SC of Cbln4-FlpO or Cdh7-FlpO mice, we can target recording from GFP-labelled SC neurons. By injecting AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE to manipulate all RGCs or AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry to manipulate specific types of RGCs into the left eye, a blue light (473 nm, 15 mW mm−2) can activate the RGC axon terminals in the SC.

Injected mice were anaesthetized by ketamine and xylazine (100 mg kg−1, 12.5 mg kg−1) and transcardially perfused with ice-cold Cutting solution (78.3 mM NaCl, 2.3 mM KCl, 33.8 mM choline-Cl, 0.45 mM CaCl2, 6.4 mM MgCl2, 1.1 mM NaH2PO4, 23 mM NaHCO3, 20 mM D-glucose, 0.5 mM L-glutamine, pH 7.4). The brains were dissected, and coronal brain sections were prepared using a vibratome (VT1200S, Leica) in ice-cold, carbogenated Cutting solution. Slices (250 μm in thickness) with SC were collected and transferred to a 32.5 °C incubation chamber filled with carbogenated Cutting solution. After 30 min incubation, the slices were transferred to room temperature artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF; 125 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 26 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM MgCl2·6H2O, 2 mM CaCl2, 20 mM D-glucose, pH 7.4) before recording. Cutting solutions and ACSF were constantly bubbled with 5% CO2 and 95% O2 (Carbogen, Airgas).

A CCD camera (IR-2000, DAGE-MTI) mounted on a fluorescence microscope (BX51WI, Olympus) was used to detect a green cell surrounded by red axon terminals. Targeted whole-cell recordings were made under IR-DIC visualization. The glass pipettes (BF150-86-10, Sutter Instrument) were pulled by a puller (P1000, Sutter Instrument) into recording electrodes (3–5 MΩ). The recording electrode was filled with potassium-based internal solutions (135 mM potassium gluconate, 8 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 0.25 mM EGTA, 2 mM MgATP, 0.3 mM Na2GTP, 7 mM phosphocreatine, pH 7.3). All data were acquired using a MultiClamp 700B Amplifier and a 1440A DigiData (Molecular Devices). The signals were digitized at 10 kHz and low-pass filtered at 1 kHz. Axon activation was performed using a 473 nm LED (Cool LED, pE300). Five light pulses (2 ms) were delivered per trial. After breaking into the cells, we held them at −65 mV and applied whole-cell compensation. Voltage-clamp mode was used to record evoked EPSCs, and current-clamp mode was used to record action potentials. Tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 µM) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 µM) were added to ACSF perfusions to confirm the monosynaptic connection. CNQX (10 µM) and APV (50 µM) were added to confirm the glutamatergic synapses. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit or random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

Recent findings suggest that an internal solution containing Biocytin (0.5%, B4261-100mg, Sigma) was used for electrophysiological recording and dye filling, as previously described71. After recording, brain slices were fixed with 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then blocked with blocking solution (PBS with 0.3% TritonX-100 and 5% normal donkey serum) for one day at 4 °C. Then the slices were incubated with Streptavidin-488 or 555 (1:1,000, Invitrogen) for 2 h at room temperature. After mounting the slices, the images were acquired by a Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM900).

In vivo calcium imaging of mouse SC was performed using a two-photon microscope as previously described72.

Surgeries were performed on eight-week-old transgenic mice. The craniotomy, virus injection, and transparent silicone plug insertion were done over the right SC. Mice were anaesthetized with ketamine and xylazine and placed in a stereotaxic device with their eyes covered with ophthalmic ointment. Mice were anaesthetized with 2% isoflurane for maintenance and injected with meloxicam (5 mg kg−1). Craniotomy was performed over the lambda of the skull, and a large flap was opened in the dura with a forceps (Dumoxel-Biology 11252-30, FST). We injected the right SC with 400 nl of AAV8-EF1α-FDIO-GCaMP6s. A silicone plug bonded to a 5 mm circular coverslip was mounted on a suction cup and positioned over the craniotomy. The plug advanced downward to press the brain and then anteriorly to displace the dura and transverse sinuses. A drop of cyanoacrylate (Vetbond, 3 M) was used to fix the silicon plug to the skull, then the suction was released, and the suction cup was withdrawn. A custom head plate (titanium, 1 mm thick, eMachineShop) was bonded to the skull by cyanoacrylate (Vetbond, 3 M) and dental cement (Ortho-Jet, LangDental). At least 2 weeks after implanting cranial windows, mice were habituated to handling and head-fixing at least 4 times under a two-photon microscope.

We imaged calcium responses in mice using a two-photon microscope (Neurolabware) with a Spectra-Physics MaiTai laser at 920 nm (15–50 mW) to excite GCaMP6s. Imaging in the SC was performed at depths of 50–200 µm below the pia surface. A 575 × 370 µm field of view was scanned at 15.5 Hz, producing a series of 416 × 268-pixel images. A tangent LCD screen (Dell, U2312HM) placed in front of the left eye of head-fixed mice will present a visual stimulus generated with Psychtoolbox3 (MATLAB) and synchronized with image acquisition via TTL signals from the stimulus screen. The screen is centred 14 cm away from the mouse, angled at 20 degrees in pitch and yaw to minimize fisheye distortion. We imaged each mouse for about 1 h, with multiple sessions on successive days if needed to present a battery of visual stimuli and acquire stable imaging.

Industry observers note that visual stimuli were presented on a tangent (1,920 × 1,080 pixels) region of the screen. The screen was strobed for 2 µs at the end of each scan line (1,200 Hz; luminance of the grey screen, 1.25 cd m−2; maximum brightness, 1/80 of the unmodified monitor) to minimize interference between the visual stimulus and two-photon fluorescence detection. All stimuli presented used only the green and blue channels of the screen. Red bars flickered periodically at the bottom of the screen, which was covered with black tape, to convey the timing of the visual stimulus to synchronize with fluorescence acquisition. All visual stimuli in two-photon experiments were presented in a pseudorandom sequence, interspersed with blank periods within each stimulus block, using a different random seed for each block. Moving gratings were used to test the direction selectivity of SC neurons. The drifting grating was 100 pixels wide (6.4°), with black or white bars, and drifted in 8 directions (45° intervals) at a speed of 356 pixels per second (22.7° per second). To map receptive fields, flashing spots were presented in a 9 × 5 position arrayed across the stimulus monitor. Each spot was a 216 × 216 pixel (13.8° × 13.8°) square that appeared for 1 second. All visual stimuli were repeated six times per trial.

Industry observers note that to test the contribution of the ipsilateral eye to the direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons, we covered the ipsilateral eye with a black box during calcium imaging. The box was removed after the experiments.

It has been revealed that we performed offline motion correction of calcium imaging data by NoRMCorre73, identified GCaMP6s+ cells, extracted calcium traces for each cell, and subtracted neuropil signals. Next, we aligned traces to visual stimuli using synchronization pulses relayed from stimulus monitors to the microscope via a TTL signal, which were time-stamped in the imaging data. For traces with high-peak noisy spikes (large mouse motion that cannot be corrected), we used a denoising algorithm to replace noisy dots with smooth traces. The noisy spike traces were determined by whether any points were bigger than the mean ± 4 s.d. traces. Then, calcium traces were aligned to the onset of each visual stimulus, averaged across trials, and the peak and valley of each mean trace were identified.

DSI calculation followed a previously published protocol74. ΔF/F values for each presentation of a stimulus were averaged from six repeats, and the peak ΔF/F for each direction was used to compute direction preference. The direction selectivity index (DSI) was calculated as the normalized amplitude of the vector sum of all directions by their scalar sum. Cells with DSI > 0.2 were classified as direction selective. The preferred direction was defined as the weighted vector sum over eight stimulus angles.

In a recent development, for confocal image acquisition, all procedures were conducted in a double-blind manner. One researcher collected images without knowledge of genotype, while a second researcher, who performed the analysis, was also blinded. Littermates were used as controls in all experiments unless otherwise indicated. Both male and female mice were included. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy) equipped with 10× air, 20× air and 40× oil immersion objectives.

To quantify immunostained cells in the SC and retina, confocal images of vertical retinal sections, coronal SC sections, and whole-mount retina were collected under identical imaging conditions across all samples. Confocal stacks of 20 µm (retina and SC sections) or 60 µm (whole-mount retina) were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Cells positive for each marker was identified using thresholded fluorescence intensity criteria. Single-positive and double-positive cells were manually counted with the Cell Counter plugin in ImageJ (NIH). For RNAscope in situ hybridization, SC sections processed with RNAscope and immunostaining were imaged on a Zeiss LSM900 with a 20× objective. The number of GFP-positive neurons or marker-positive cells was counted across all stained samples as mentioned above. Data were pooled across animals, and results are presented as percentages (mean ± s.e.m.). Confocal image files for histology were analysed using Fiji Image J (v1.53c), Microsoft Excel 365, Graph Pad Prism9, Adobe Illustrator 2020. Electrophysiological data collection and analysis were not performed blindly with respect to the experimental conditions. All whole-cell recording data were acquired by Camplex 10.7 (Molecular Devices) and analysed in MATLAB (MathWorks) or Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices). Optogenetically evoked currents were averaged across 5 trials. Clampfit 10.7 measured the peak amplitudes of evoked currents. MATLAB analysed the intrinsic properties of recorded neurons. All statistics were calculated by GraphPad Prism 9. Peak currents between the two groups were compared using a two-tailed Student’s t-test.

According to recent reports, optomotor response was described previously75. The OptoDrum (Striatech) comprises a box with four screens to simulate drifting gratings. An IR camera mounted on the top of the box was used to record mouse movements. Mice were first acclimated to the room in their cages for 30 min. Then, freely moving mice were placed on a platform and allowed to acclimate to the box for at least 5 min. Drifting gratings (12° s−1) in the clockwise direction can trigger left-eye-mediated body and head movements, while drifting gratings in the counterclockwise direction were used to test right-eye-mediated movements. Drifting gratings were presented from low spatial frequencies (0.056 cycles per degree) to high frequencies (0.3–0.5 cycles per degree) to determine the threshold at which a mouse could track. OptoDrum’s software can detect the body shape of mice and label the positions of head, body, and tail of mice. The stimulus and video tracking were paused if a mouse engaged in grooming behaviour or dropped off the platform and resumed later. The software can score the optomotor response and determine the spatial-frequency threshold. False positives were manually identified as invalid, and the same frequency of drifting gratings was repeated. We compared the spatial-frequency threshold of drifting gratings to trigger optomotor responses in the left eye (ablation) with the right eye (control) to assess visual acuity differences.

Recent findings suggest that we obtained measurements from distinct biological samples. No covariates were tested. No formal test of normality was performed; statistical tests were selected based on the distributional assumptions of the data. Statistical methods and the number of animals tested for each configuration are documented in the figure legends for each experiment. When comparing two groups, statistics were derived using an unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test or Fisher’s exact test, as indicated in the figure legends. For comparing cell-type proportions across multiple reactions, we used the Kruskal–Wallis H test (scipy.stats.kruskal, Python). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed in GraphPad Prism 9 to assess the statistical significance of differences among multiple measurements.

Fisher’s exact test was performed using the Easy Fisher Exact Test Calculator (https://www.socscistatistics.com/tests/fisher/default2.aspx).

According to recent reports, statistical significance was defined as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001. All values indicate mean ± s.e.m., unless otherwise noted.

In a recent development, a, Unsupervised classification of sSC using the standard fresh-frozen MERFISH protocol. UMAP embedding of 5,845 cells reveals consistent clustering of the same 8 ENCs and 11 INCs identified with TransA-MERFISH on fixed tissue (Fig. 1d). Cell-type labels were assigned to Leiden clusters based on canonical marker gene expression patterns and transcriptomic mapping via a supervised XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH atlas. b, Confusion matrix showing transcriptomic correspondence between cell types in standard MERFISH (rows) and TransA-MERFISH (columns). c, Violin plots comparing quality control metrics between standard MERFISH (blue) and TransA-MERFISH (gray). Distributions are highly similar across key metrics, including the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts), total transcript counts per cell (total_counts), and cell mask area (in pixels). A modest reduction in n_genes_by_counts and total_counts was observed in TransA-MERFISH experiments. d, Comparison of matched neuronal subtype frequencies between standard MERFISH and TransA-MERFISH. Values are plotted on a ln-ln scale to highlight low-frequency types. A strong correlation is observed across both excitatory and inhibitory populations, indicating that the TransA-MERFISH protocol did not bias or deplete neuron types in the sSC (Pearson R = 0.88). e, Validation accuracies of the XGBoost classifier trained using various gene selection strategies: the performance of the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel was compared to randomly sampled 140-gene sets drawn from either the full single-cell transcriptome or the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs). Additional gene sets were constructed by selecting the top k specific genes (Methods) per SC neuronal cluster (k = 1–10), based on 19 neuronal clusters identified from re-clustering of the neuronal subset of the dataset28. Data are presented as mean ± SD. f, Dot plots comparing the expression patterns of 2 non-optimal probes (top row, blue) with their corresponding expressions in snRNA-seq17 (bottom row, orange). MERFISH cells are grouped according to their predicted snRNA-seq cluster identities, as inferred by Tangram-based imputation (Methods). The 140-gene list is presented in Supplementary Table 1. g-j, Classification and filtering of non-neuron cells (NNs). UMAP embedding (g) of all high-quality cells (47740 cells after quality filtering, see Methods) before filtering out non-neuronal cells, colored by broad cell classes: excitatory neurons (ENCs), inhibitory neurons (INCs), and NNs. NNs were identified using a supervised XGBoost classifier (i) trained on an SC snRNA-seq dataset, as in the reference28. Violin plots (h) of quality control metrics show that NNs exhibit reduced numbers of detected genes per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts per cell (total_counts), consistent with the design principles for neurons in the TransA-MERFISH gene panel. Bar plots (j) showing the average proportions of ENCs and INCs among all detected cells across animals. NNs were subsequently filtered out before re-clustering of neuronal cells to improve classification resolution among neuronal types. n = 16 animals. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

a,b, Transcriptomic correspondence between the MERFISH-based sSC neuron atlas and the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (CCN20230722; Allen Institute)20. (a) UMAP embedding of the TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), colored by the most probable mapped supertype identity inferred via MapMyCells. (b) Confusion matrix showing the correspondence between TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (rows) and 10 x WMB supertypes (columns), as determined by MapMyCells mapping (Methods). c, Transcriptomic correspondence between the TransA-MERFISH sSC neuron atlas and the Trans-Seq single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) SC neuron atlas9, as determined by XGBoost-based classification (Methods). Dot size and color represent the proportion of cells from each Trans-Seq cluster (y-axis) mapped to the corresponding TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (x-axis), indicating the scRNA-seq-based protocol biases a few neuronal subsets due to the nature of the dissociation and FACS sorting, thus it is not optimal to represent adult neuron clusters precisely and comprehensively. d, Dot plot comparing transcriptomic signatures of representative neuronal types across three datasets: TransA-MERFISH (red), single-nucleus RNA-seq (green)22, and supertypes from the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (blue; corresponding to panels a,b). Shown are selected excitatory neuron types—including Cdh7+ SC neurons (ENC1, ENC2), Npnt+ wide-field SC neurons (ENC5), and Etv1+ SC neurons (ENC6)—as well as inhibitory neuron types, including Cbln4+ SC neurons (INC1) and Fibcd1+ SC neurons (INC3). The consistent expression patterns of key marker genes across datasets support the robustness of cell classification in the TransA-MERFISH atlas and align with mapping results obtained via machine learning (g,j) and MapMyCells (a,b). e-j, Alignments of the TransA-MERFISH neuronal clusters with past single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-Seq) atlases of the mouse SC, indicating consistency across datasets. Re-clustering of neuronal subsets from reference datasets reproduced the original cell-type assignments (e17 and h22). Confusion matrices (f,i) show that XGBoost models trained on the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel achieve high validation accuracy in recovering snRNA-seq-defined cell types. Heatmaps (g,j) show the transcriptomic correspondence between snRNA-seq cell clusters (y-axis) and the TransA-MERFISH types (x-axis), based on predictions from an XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH dataset using the 140 genes. Color intensity reflects the percentage of cells from each snRNA-seq cluster mapped to each TransA-MERFISH type.

Recent findings suggest that a-b, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with cells colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (a), and split UMAP embedding for each replicate separately (b), showing consistent cluster structure across replicates. c, Histograms display consistent percentages of neurons for each dataset contributing to each identified neuron type, for a stable representation of cell types across datasets. d, Violin plots showing the distributions of the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts detected per cell (total counts) across each of the 19 sSC neuronal types. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. f, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with mWmC+ neurons colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (as in panel a). g, UMAP distribution for each of the three datasets separately, showing that all mWmC+ types have contributions from three reactions. e, Stacked barplot highlights consistent mWmC+ labeling of each retino-recipient neuron type across datasets, ensuring a stable representation of retino-recipient cell types. h, Bar plots showing the proportions of each cell type across the three replicates. Comparisons across tracing conditions using the Kruskal–Wallis test revealed no differences among cell types (p > 0.05). Data are presented as mean ± SD. i, left, Example of raw MERFISH images with DAPI (gray) and RNA transcripts (blue); colored segmented cell masks are generated using a customized Cellpose 2.0 model. middle, Similar to (left) but overlapped with curated colored masks annotated manually as a benchmark. right, Comparison of Cellpose model-generated masks and curated masks. Light green shows true positive (TP), pink show False Positive (FP), and purple show False Negative (FN). j, Violin plot showing the performance score across three animals. Calculation of precision, recall and F1 are as following: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2 * Precision * Recall / (Precision + Recall). The horizontal line within the violin indicates the median. k, Violin plot showing the distribution of Intersection over Union (IoU) across animals and images. Violin plots show the distribution of the data. The centre line indicates the median, and the lower and upper bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, respectively.

a-e, Consistent dorsal-ventral cluster distribution along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes. Sample images (a) showing the spatial distribution of cell clusters within each slice across the anterior-posterior axis. Compositional distribution of different neuron clusters (b, excitatory; c, inhibitory) across the anterior-to-posterior axis. Compositional distribution of different neuronal clusters (d, excitatory; e, inhibitory) along the medial-to-lateral axis. n = 16 animals. f-g, Sample images showing sublaminar distribution for each ENC (f) or INC (g) along the dorsal-ventral axis of the sSC. The somata median positions along the dorsal-ventral axis are plotted for all ENC and INC (Fig. 1f). Colored lines are the mean; gray lines are individual measurements. Scale bars, 100 μm.

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic of strategy to examine selective connectivity from all RGCs (AAV2-ChR2-YFP, green) to SC neurons (either SC-FlpO; FSF-RFP or SC-Cre; FSF-RFP, red) using CRACM. b-d, CRACM experiments show findings consistent with those from TransA-MERFISH, in which RGCs innervate ENC5 (Npnt+, b) but not ENC6 (Etv1+, c). Amplitudes of evoked currents and percentages of innervations were quantified in (d). n = 4 animals; 7 out of 13 ENC5 were connected, 2 out of 9 ENC6 were weakly innervated. *p = 0.0478, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. e-h, Experimental scheme (e) for findings in (Fig. 1k) using immunohistochemistry indicates co-staining with anti-RFP and anti-Npnt antibodies (f,h, n = 4 animals; 128 neurons), whereas no co-localization was observed between goat anti-RFP and rabbit anti-Etv1 antibodies (g,h, n = 4 animals; 103 neurons). (h) Statistical results for f,g. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. ***p = 0.0002, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. j-k, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in ENC1 and ENC2 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Dotted yellow circles indicate in situ signals that overlap with GFP staining. n = 4 biologically independent animals. Cbln4 expression (red) is exclusive of Cdh7-GFP (green) (n), as quantified in (o). n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars, 50 μm. p-q, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in ENC1 and ENC2 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Itga7 (red, ENC1) and Sntb1 (blue, ENC2) are mutually exclusive in Cdh7-GFP SC neurons (p), as quantified in (q). ENC1 and ENC2 each account for 50% and 25% of the total GFP neurons, respectively, while neither Itga7 nor Sntb1 overlaps. n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars, 50 μm. Bradford City 2 Doncaster Rovers 2: Second-half fracas lights fuse to dramatic final quarter

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • City suffered a wretched derby loss to Huddersfield Town, while Rovers were eviscerated at MK Dons, with another ghastly experience seven days later at Kidderminster Harriers, in the FA Cup, compounding their woes.
  • It was a big afternoon for good friends Michael Duff and Grant McCann, with the latter being under the pump with supporters following recent events.
  • Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

City suffered a wretched derby loss to Huddersfield Town, while Rovers were eviscerated at MK Dons, with another ghastly experience seven days later at Kidderminster Harriers, in the FA Cup, compounding their woes.

It was a big afternoon for good friends Michael Duff and Grant McCann, with the latter being under the pump with supporters following recent events.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The fuse for a hitherto pretty quiet derby was lit by an on-pitch fracas involving Kieran Morgan and George Broadbent in the second period, with both benches clashing - and Duff and McCann copping bookings in the process.

It was the precursor to a riproaring final quarter. McCann was the one smiling at the death.

Rovers’ winger Jordan Thomas cancelled out Nick Powell’s 55th-minute opener with a fantastic overhead kick on 74 minutes.

But the visitors then suffered dismay four minutes later when substitute Stephen Humphrys drilled home an emphatic winner.

There was time for a final twist in the fifth minute of stoppage-time when Sean Grehan headed home unmarked following Robbie Gotts’ corner. It was not the sort of concession that Duff likes.

Morgan and Powell were handed their first league starts of the campaign for Bradford, while Josh Neufville, out since September 19 with hamstring trouble, was a significant returnee.

Keighley’s Matty Pearson was a noteworthy inclusion for Rovers, in his first league start since September 6 and only his second in 2026-27 following a calf injury and double hernia operation.

A rusty challenge inside the first 25 seconds on Powell saw Pearson cop a quick-fire yellow card, placing him on a tightrope for the rest of the game.

According to recent reports, city had slightly the better of it in a low-incident first half, which smacked of classic derby fare. The goalless scoreline at the interval was just fine given recent events for Rovers, that mentioned.

They were diligent and competitive, which was a step in the right direction given Aggborough and Stadium MK and a scruffy sort of game also suited them in the circumstances.

Rare as they were, scares on goal were provided by those in claret and amber, who boasted 67.6 per cent possession.

Powell planted a meaty header wide under pressure following an inviting cross from Neufville, who fancied it down the right against Jordan Thomas when the chance arose.

Later on in the half, alert covering defence denied Jackson a clean connection when well placed after being found by Antoni Sarcevic following an eye-catching backheel close to the byline from Powell.

At the other end, Rovers had a couple of half-decent movements down the sides, but there were relatively few alarms for the home defence.

Recent findings suggest that going the other way, the onus was on City to do a bit more on the resumption, playing in front of the Kop - and be a touch quicker to pull Rovers out of their shape without the ball. They needed a spark and it would arrive on 55 minutes.

Callum Connolly’s juicy cross on the right saw Powell get in between a couple of defenders before confidently steering a well-placed header past Tommy Simkin.

The onus was on Rovers to throw a bit more caution to the wind.

Speaking of caution, both McCann and Duff saw incurred the ire of referee Darren Drysdale with emotions following a fracas in the box between Morgan and Broadbent, who had a pop at each other in the box, sparking a kerfuffle between both sets of players.

A low-grade derby was finally getting spiced up.

A brilliant reaction save from Simkin then denied substitute Humphrys after Pennington flicked on Ibou Touray’s right-wing corner before a huge chance at the other end saw Thomas cut inside and fire a low shot inches wide.

Rovers, who made a triple change with James Collins on for his debut alongside Alfie May and Leon Ayinde, started to up it.

Thomas knocked on wood with a first-time volley from Broadbent’s corner before persistence paid off for the winger, firing home splendidly after Collins knock-down.

Rovers' joy was short-lived with replacement Will Swan spotting Humphrys in space and his drilled finish was inch-perfect.

Sources indicate that simkin was then forced into more work to turn away Humphrys’ fierce drive. But Grehan had the final word.

It has been revealed that bradford City: McCracken; Pennington, Baldwin, Pratt (Gillesphey 85); Neufville (Swan 65), Connolly, Morgan (Phillips 77); Touray; Sarcevic, Jackson; Powell (Humphrys 64). Substitutes unused: O’Keeffe, Matthews, Hadi.

Doncaster Rovers: Simkin; Nixon (Ayinde 66), Grehan, Pearson (Adelakun 80), Senior; Bailey, Broadbent (Byrne 80); Gotts, Hutchinson (May 66), Thomas; Hanlan (Collins 67). Substitutes unused: Clarke, Robinson.

Attendance: 19,836 (1,371 Doncaster Rovers fans).

Industry News: Ajax vs. ADO Den Haag - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 19:45, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:50.
  • ADO Den Haag travel to the Johan Cruyff Arena on Sunday, looking to end their six-match losing run against Amsterdam giants Ajax in this weekend's matchday 13 Eredivisie encounter.
  • Their 15-year wait for victory in this fixture further underlines the magnitude of the task facing Maurice Steijn's side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 19:45, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:50.

ADO Den Haag travel to the Johan Cruyff Arena on Sunday, looking to end their six-match losing run against Amsterdam giants Ajax in this weekend's matchday 13 Eredivisie encounter.

Their 15-year wait for victory in this fixture further underlines the magnitude of the task facing Maurice Steijn's side.

Ajax entered the recent international break wondering what might have been after surrendering a two-goal advantage at FC Twente.

Goals from Tolu Arokodare and substitute Rayane Bounida seemingly put Michel's men home and hosed heading into the final half-hour, only for Dies Janse to score an own goal and Wout Weghorst to punish his former side with a penalty in the fifth minute of second-half stoppage time.

That equaliser denied De Joden the opportunity to finish gameweek 12 atop the Eredivisie table, leaving them level on 25 points with Feyenoord and one behind leaders PSV Eindhoven, who are chasing a fourth consecutive title.

Looking to move on from that setback, the Amsterdam giants welcome ADO to the capital aiming to secure a seventh consecutive victory over the promoted side.

Further encouraging the hosts is their longstanding unbeaten record in this fixture, with a 3-2 defeat in March 2011 marking Ajax's last loss to this weekend's visitors.

ADO have since gone 20 competitive meetings without a victory in this fixture, losing 15 times to underline their historical inferiority.

As such, it will be intriguing to see how latest boss Steijn approaches his first match in charge of the promoted side, who dismissed Robin Peter before the international break following a run of one victory in 11 Eredivisie matches.

There was an immediate lift under Levi Schwiebbe as the second-bottom outfit defeated Sparta Rotterdam 3-1 to move within one point of 16th-placed Telstar in the relegation playoff spot and two of SBV Excelsior.

Back-to-back top-flight victories could therefore lift Den Haag out of the relegation positions, although results elsewhere must also go their way.

Despite the managerial change, ADO's away record offers little encouragement, with the visitors collecting just two points from an available 18 on their travels and failing to score in three of those six matches.

Those figures, coupled with their historical struggles against Ajax, underline the challenge facing Steijn, who is winless in 15 previous encounters with the capital club, losing 11.

ADO Den Haag form (all competitions):.

Ajax could again be without Julian Brandt this weekend, with the attacking midfielder having not played since going off injured in late October's 1-0 victory over AZ Alkmaar.

If the six-goal Germany international remains sidelined, Arokodare, who has seven goals and one assist, will shoulder much of the attacking responsibility, while Oscar Gloukh offers a creative threat with six assists, including setting up both goals in the 2-2 draw at Twente a fortnight ago.

While Anton Gaaei, like Brandt, will be assessed before Sunday, Michel must manage without Simon Adingra, long-term absentee Kasper Dolberg (knee) and Viktor Tsygankov.

Steijn has fewer injury concerns, although the ADO boss must make do without Alex Pozo and Luka Reischl (groin) this weekend.

Juho Kilo may not score regularly, but the midfielder's passing and creativity make him a standout presence for the visitors.

Nonetheless, the goalscoring burden falls on Nigel Thomas, Yannick Eduardo and Evan Rottier, who have netted four, three and two league goals respectively.

Ter Stegen; Rosa, Bouman, Janse, Wijndal; Amrabat, Baas; Klaassen, Mokio, Gloukh; Arokodare.

ADO Den Haag possible starting lineup:.

Nikiema; De Ruijter, Mulder, Waem, Hokke; Kilo, Jimenez; Van Mieghem, Rottier, Hawkins; Thomas.

Ajax's late collapse at Twente demonstrated that their defensive concentration remains fallible, offering some hope to an ADO side fresh from scoring three against Sparta.

Nevertheless, Gloukh's creativity and Arokodare's finishing should give Michel's men enough attacking quality to overcome Brandt's potential absence and prolong the visitors' miserable record in this fixture.
