Latest Update: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (9966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section.
  • According to recent reports, the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7.
  • For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections1,2,3, and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips4. In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model5. The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

According to recent reports, the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7. In superfluids and superconductors, this breaking manifests in the emergence of a macroscopic condensate that exhibits long-range phase coherence. This coherence is ultimately responsible for properties such as dissipationless transport8,9, the Josephson effect10, and in the case of superconductivity the Meissner effect11. Although relatively robust in bulk systems, in lower-dimensional systems, the enhanced effect of fluctuations—and in particular topological defects—can suppress this long-range phase coherence and govern superfluid transport4,12.

For example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts. The supercurrent, proportional to this gradient, would grow without bound unless intermittent phase fluctuations relax the accumulated gradient. By relaxing the gradient, the fluctuations dissipate energy, thereby causing a resistance3,13. The characteristics of the fluctuations and their corresponding resistance depend on the dimensionality of the setup as follows.

Industry observers note that in one-dimensional (1D) wires, discrete relaxation events known as phase slips dominate the dynamics. Microscopically, a phase slip occurs when the magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is transiently and locally suppressed over a healing length ξ. Where the amplitude vanishes, the phase is ill-defined, allowing for phase jumps of 2π. As the order parameter recovers, the wire returns to a state with a uniform amplitude but a reduced phase gradient4 (Fig. 1a, top row).

a, Dissipation in a narrow, quasi-1D channel occurs because of phase slips, in which a depletion of the order parameter allows for a relaxation of the phase gradient and kinetic energy (top row). The corresponding phase (colour-coded) evolution of a phase slip in a narrow channel is plotted in the central row. In a wide, quasi-2D channel, dissipation is governed by vortex–antivortex pairs traversing the channel (bottom row). b, A transport channel of programmable width connects two superfluid reservoirs (blue). The channel is formed by two repulsive beams (green and orange), one of which is tunable by a DMD.

According to recent reports, in two-dimensional (2D) geometries, such as thin films, dissipation instead arises from the nucleation and motion of topological defects known as vortices. A vortex is a point-like singularity of the phase around which the phase winds by 2π, with a small core in which the amplitude is suppressed. Driven by a current, vortices move across the film and dissipate energy. Each time a vortex traverses the sample, the phase difference between the contacts relaxes by 2π. Repeated vortex crossings generate a finite voltage and hence an effective resistance14,15 (Fig. 1a, bottom row). In intermediate, thin-strip geometries, both vortex flow and phase slips may contribute to dissipation.

Industry observers note that previous studies included experiments on superconducting rings16; Dayem-bridge nanowires17,18,19,20; Bose–Einstein condensates in dumbbell21,22, cylindrical23 or toroidal geometries24; optical lattices25,26; and fermionic Josephson junctions27,28,29. These previous studies have explored various facets of phase-slip and vortex physics, including direct imaging of vortices28,30,31,32, the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition33 and the recent observation of Shapiro steps in atomic Josephson junctions34,35. However, the experimental challenge of isolating and characterizing geometric or dimensional effects on dissipation remains unresolved.

With the rise of quantum simulation of devices based on highly controllable ultracold atomic gases36,37, it is now possible to shed upcoming light on how these dissipative processes emerge in quantum systems.

According to recent reports, in this work, we use ultracold, strongly interacting fermions in a two-terminal configuration to study nonlinear transport through a digitally programmable channel. The optically shaped channel can be reproducibly tuned from a quasi-1D to a quasi-2D geometry, providing a platform ideally suited for probing the influence of geometry on fluctuation-driven dissipation in the absence of defects or impurities.

It has been revealed that in the narrow, 1D channel limit, we identify signatures of phase slips, in agreement with the Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin (LAMH) theory4,38,39. In particular, we observe the predicted exponential suppression of the LAMH activation factor over many orders of magnitude on widening the channel. For even larger widths, the system crosses over to a 2D regime in which dissipation is dominated by vortices, as indicated by the observed power-law dependence of the current–voltage characteristics predicted for vortex dynamics.

It has been revealed that beyond establishing these limiting behaviours, our measurements provide a direct window into the crossover between 1D and 2D transport, a regime in which analytical modelling is challenging. It is in this crossover that widening the channel paradoxically increases its resistance. More broadly, our results highlight the utility of ultracold atomic superfluids as a platform for quantum simulation of nonequilibrium transport.

Sources indicate that we prepare a balanced mixture of the lowest and third-lowest hyperfine states of fermionic 6Li in the unitary regime. A total of 2N = 2.7 ± 0.1 × 105 atoms are cooled to T/TF = 0.144 ± 0.007, where N denotes the number of atom pairs, TF denotes the Fermi temperature, and the errors in both quantities denote the uncertainties due to shot-to-shot fluctuations. The temperature corresponds to T/TC ≈ 0.7, where TC ≈ 0.2TF denotes the critical temperature40. The atoms are confined in a cigar-shaped, harmonic trap with trapping frequencies (νx, νy, νz) = (222 ± 7, 28.1 ± 0.1, 195 ± 5) Hz.

Sources indicate that as shown in Fig. 1a, a repulsive TEM0,1 beam, propagating in the x-direction, is aligned with the trap centre. It divides the atomic cloud into two reservoirs, separated by a quasi-2D transport region that is 51 ± 1 μm long and provides confinement of ν2D = 10.46 ± 0.09 kHz along z. Within the central 27 ± 0.5 μm of this plane, the atoms are further confined in the x-direction to a channel of variable width w. The channel is defined by a repulsive beam propagating along z, shaped by a digital micromirror device (DMD). It enables reproducible tunability of w from 0.9 ± 0.5 μm to 19.8 ± 0.5 μm, in which the uncertainty is dominated by and calculated from the resolution limit of our projection system (numerical aperture = 0.53, λ = 532 nm). Note that given the dimensions of our setup, we are not in the Josephson regime (see Methods, ‘No Josephson oscillations’). A third, attractive Gaussian beam (not shown) illuminates the transport channel and its connections to the reservoirs, locally increasing the degeneracy. A more detailed description of this effect as well as of the overall setup can be found in ref. 41.

At time t = 0, we prepare a relative atom-pair imbalance between the two reservoirs, ΔN/N = (Nl − Nr)/(Nl + Nr), where Nl,r denote the number of atom pairs in the left and right reservoirs. An initial imbalance of ΔN/N ≈ 0.1 relaxes through an approximately constant initial current, followed by damped oscillations of the imbalance. The discharge is distinctly non-exponential, indicating a nonlinear response. The damping, and in particular its dependence on the channel width w, carries information about the underlying microscopic mechanisms.

The key data of our measurement series are shown in Fig. 2a. We record transport traces for w between 0.9 ± 0.5 μm and 19.8 ± 0.5 μm. As w increases, the magnitude of the initial current increases, which manifests in a steeper initial slope. Concurrently, both the oscillation frequency and amplitude grow. The frequency rises from just below 10 Hz to approximately 18 Hz (see also Extended Data Fig. 1). For the narrowest channel (w = 0.9 ± 0.5 μm), the oscillation amplitude is comparable to the noise floor and barely resolved. By contrast, for the widest channel (w = 19.8 ± 0.5 μm), the amplitude reaches ΔN/N ≈ 0.06.

According to recent reports, a, Atom transport (imbalance ΔN/N as a function of time t) of a unitary Fermi gas through channels of increasing width shows distinctively changing dissipation characteristics. The data are compared with fitted phase slip (LAMH) and vortex models. The models both describe the TNR in the circuit (b), capturing either phase slips or vortices. The LAMH model fits narrow channels, whereas the vortex model fits wide channels. The measurements for different channel widths are vertically offset for clarity. The statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically four to five measurements per data point) are smaller than the marker size. c, A quality-of-fit \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis substantiates the change of the dominant model apparent in a.

Recent findings suggest that the damping exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on w. At longer transport times (for example, t = 0.3 s), the remaining oscillation amplitude reaches a maximum for intermediate channel widths (see also Fig. 4). These signals suggest distinct dissipative mechanisms in the narrow and wide channel limits, which we analyse quantitatively below.

The general characteristics of the dynamics can be understood as arising from the interplay between the potential energy stored in the reservoirs, the kinetic energy inside the channel and the dissipative processes we want to investigate. To study these dissipative processes, we model our system with an equivalent RLC circuit shown in Fig. 2b. We first characterize the capacitance and inductance of the circuit to subsequently infer the dissipative (resistive) processes by fitting the dynamics of the circuit to the measurements. The capacitances, inductance and resistance in the circuit model correspond to the compressibility of the atomic reservoirs, the inertia of the atoms and the dissipative processes in the channel, respectively. We explore these elements in the following starting with the capacitors. As the model circuit features two capacitors in series, each with a capacitance C, the effective capacitance of the circuit is Ceff = C/2. The compressibility κeff of the gas allows to quantify this equivalent capacitance Ceff (potential energy per atom pair displaced from equilibrium) through \(\frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{\kappa }_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathrm{pot}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{C}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). We measured the compressibility of our sample (Methods, ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) to find hCeff = 15.8 ± 0.5 s, where h is Planck’s constant. Next we quantify the inductance. To do so, we assume all channels have box-like potentials. A charge-neutral atom-pair current I carries a kinetic energy Ekin that depends on w. We define the inductance of our systems using \({E}_{{\rm{kin}}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}L{I}^{2}.\) We developed a model that predicts a functional dependence.

(Methods, ‘Derivation of the inductance’). By analysing the oscillation frequencies observed in our measurements and noting that in a weakly damped circuit, the frequencies are given by \(\omega (w)\approx 1/\sqrt{L(w){C}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), we find ℓc/h = 3.01 ± 0.03 × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06 ± 0.04 × 10−6 s. Although the details are provided in the Supplementary Information, here we state that the first term in equation (1) captures the kinetic energy in the channel, whereas the second term accounts for the kinetic energy in the reservoirs.

Phase slips and vortices dissipate the kinetic energy of the current into heat. So, they effectively act as a topological nonlinear resistor (TNR). With L and C determined, the resistance R remains the sole unknown component in our circuit. Owing to the nature of phase slips, R is topological and nonlinear, meaning it depends not only on the geometry but also on the current.

Sources indicate that showing how R depends on geometry, in particular in relation to the length scale given by ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’), reveals the nature of the underlying dissipative processes. To do so, we fit the width-dependent resistance R(w) in the equations of motion of an RLC circuit (derived in Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’).

For narrow, quasi-1D channels (w ≱ 2ξ), we expect the system to be in the phase slip regime. The LAMH model predicts4.

According to recent reports, defined using R = V/I, where R0 is the characteristic resistance, w0 is the characteristic width, and I0 = 2kBT/h, where kB is the Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature. The exponential suppression of R with w reflects the thermally activated phase-slip rate scaling with \(\varGamma \propto \exp (-\Delta F/({k}_{{\rm{B}}}T))\) (ref. 18), where the free energy barrier for phase slips is ΔF ∝ w. The sinh(I/I0) term can intuitively be understood as follows: at small |I/I0| ≪ 1, phase slips occur in both directions with roughly equal probability; as the bias increases slightly, phase slips that relax the current become more probable. For large |I/I0| ≫ 1, sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2. reflecting the local destabilization of the superfluid and the resulting exponential increase in the phase-slip probability.

Sources indicate that using our predetermined C and L(w), we determine R0 and w0 by fitting them simultaneously to the measurements of our four narrowest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’). Assuming that the LAMH model can be used to describe our system, a simultaneous fit to multiple channel widths provides a robust extraction of the model parameters but enforces the predicted exponential suppression of RLAMH with w. We find R0/h = 102.3±0.2 and w0 = 49.7(6) nm, where the errors denote the uncertainties of the fit. The resulting fits (shown in Fig. 2a) largely capture the dynamics for channels with a width up to w = 2.5 μm. This is quantified by \(\mathrm{NRMSE}\,=\) \(\sqrt{{\sum }_{i}{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}/N}/({m}_{\max }-{m}_{\min }) < 0.06\), where mi and fi denote the measured and fitted imbalances, respectively, and mmax − mmin is the measured signal range. However, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis \(({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 9)\) shown in Fig. 2c suggests additional systematic effects beyond the very small statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically on the level of 0.004). These systematic effects could originate from the approximation of modelling the channel with a box-like potential or the attractive beam illuminating the channel locally increasing the temperature. Outside the validity range of the model, the quality of the fits degrades noticeably, failing to capture the phase of the oscillations and underestimating their damping.

In a second step, we validate the choice of the LAMH model by fitting RLAMH(w) to each curve individually. In contrast to the simultaneous fit, these individual fits do not enforce the predicted scaling RLAMH(w) and therefore provide an independent test of whether the scaling is present in the data. Within the validity regime of the model, the individual fits reproduce the predicted exponential scaling over many orders of magnitude, as shown in Fig. 3a.

Industry observers note that a, The fitted phase-slip resistance RLAMH(w), for narrow channels, shows the exponential suppression with width, as predicted by LAMH theory. b, The fitted vortex resistivity ρv(w), for wide channels, shows the predicted power law. Inside the crossover region (2–4ξ), that is, outside the validity range of the models, both scalings break down (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’). Note that a and b display different quantities (resistance compared with resistivity) characterizing different regimes (1D compared with 2D) and are therefore not intended to be compared across the dimensional crossover. The error bars represent the error of the fit.

In a recent development, this is the first main finding of this paper. Compared with RLAMH(w), the total resistance R(I, w) apparent in the measurements (Fig. 2a) varies much less. As we initialize a fixed potential bias in our system, the exponential geometric suppression (R ∝ exp(−w/w0)) approximately cancels the current-induced exponential enhancement (R ∝ sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2). This allows RLAMH to be inferred over a wide range—more than 10 decades—while only exploring a relatively modest dynamic range of R. Importantly, the observed scaling of RLAMH(w) is contained within the data itself and is not just an artefact of the choice of the model. This becomes evident when the model is applied outside its validity regime, where the scaling breaks down immediately (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’).

In quasi-2D channels (w ≳ 4ξ), phase slips become energetically unfavourable, as their activation energy increases exponentially with w. Instead, dissipation is expected to be governed by vortex flow. Owing to the vortices, we expect to see a power-law dependence in the pair-current density J:.

Recent findings suggest that where J0 = I0/ξ. A derivation, building on the results of ref. 5, is provided in the Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’. By fitting α and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) simultaneously to the data of our four widest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’), we find \(\alpha =1.98\pm 0.04,{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \sim }}_{0}/h=1{0}^{-4.79\pm 0.07}\). As apparent from Fig. 2a, this model captures the dynamics for channels in the 2D regime (NRMSE ≱ 0.06). In these cases, \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 4\). Note that the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, and for wide channels, the box-potential approximation is safer compared with narrow channels. Apart from these statistical tests, we validate our model by fixing α to its global fit value but fitting ρv to each individual curve. Within the validity range of the model, these individual fits agree with the predicted power-law ρv ∝ wα−1 (Fig. 3b). This scaling is the second main finding of the paper. The scaling breaks down outside the validity regime of the model (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’), providing evidence that the observed scaling is a feature of the data, not a mere artefact of the enforced power law R ∝ Jα−1. When approaching the dimensional crossover w ≱ 4ξ, while still largely capturing the dynamics, the model begins to slightly but systematically underestimate the amplitude of the oscillations at long times. Presumably, because the approximation of sufficiently large w used in the derivation of R(J) ceases to hold (Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’). The eventual breakdown of the vortex model at w ≈ 4ξ marks the end of the 2D regime: the vortex model should be valid only when vortex–antivortex pairs are available as excitations. As each vortex has a radius of ξ, such an excitation requires w ≳ 4ξ. This leaves a gap between the validity ranges of the phase slip and the vortex model, in which neither model provides a microscopically satisfactory description. In this gap, there is a dimensional crossover, in which both phase slips and vortices compete.

The underdamped oscillations allow us to characterize dissipation in our system using only a few basic assumptions, while staying agnostic to the dissipation mechanism. This is particularly useful to analyse the dimensional crossover, in which neither the phase-slip nor the vortex model provide a satisfactory microscopical description. We split the total energy Etot into a potential (capacitive) energy EC and a kinetic (inductive) energy EL. We assume Etot = EC(ΔN) + EL(I, w) with EC ∝ ΔN2 and EL(I = 0, w) = 0. For each channel width w, we extract the times ti,w at which ΔN(t = ti, w) reaches an extremum and thus I ≈ 0. There, the system has minimal inductive energy (EL ≈ 0) and maximal capacitive energy. The fraction of the initial energy remaining in the system is then given by.

In a recent development, the remaining energy as a function of time and channel width is shown in Fig. 4. The plot is obtained by cubic interpolation between the measured points, performed linearly in time and logarithmically in width.

The remaining energy in the oscillator paradoxically varies non-monotonically as a function of the channel width w. For a given time after the initial decay, the maximum appears in the crossover region, near w = 4 μm ≈ 3ξ, in which phase slips and vortices are suppressed but competing. The crosses mark the measurement points (typically four to five measurements per cross) between which we interpolate. We estimate the individual data points to have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a statistical uncertainty smaller than 2% (Methods, ‘Error estimation’).

For a fixed width, the energy decays over time, reflecting dissipation. At any given time t > 0.15 s, Et(w)/E0 varies non-monotonically with the channel width, exhibiting a clear maximum near w ≈ 3ξ, corresponding to a minimal effective resistance. We call this deviation from the expected monotonicity the ‘quantum resistance paradox’ and consider it the third and last main finding of this paper. Note that the activation energy for phase slips increases exponentially with channel width, whereas vortex–antivortex pairs require sufficiently wide channels to form. The observed non-monotonicity thus suggests a transition in the underlying dissipation mechanism and a crossover from 1D to 2D physics.

We have investigated atom transport between two bulk superfluids through channels across different dimensional regimes and observed distinct behaviours. In narrow, quasi-1D channels, our data are in agreement with those of the LAMH model. We infer the geometric suppression of the phase slips by many orders of magnitude, providing the first experimental confirmation of the predicted geometric scaling. For wide, quasi-2D channels, dissipation is captured by a vortex flow model. The borders of the 1D and 2D regimes appear close to the theoretically expected length scale. A measurement of energy decay, agnostic to microscopic details, provides further evidence for a transition in the dissipation mechanism for channels of intermediate width, which paradoxically exhibit the least energy loss. These findings not only suggest routes for optimizing energy transport in mesoscopic devices but also provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts to describe the delicate phase-slip and vortex-flow mechanisms in the dimensional crossover in superfluids and superconductors42,43,44.

Our setup is analogous to an RLC circuit with the mapping presented in Extended Data Table 1.

In a recent development, the procedures for determining the capacitance C and the inductance L are described in sections ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’ and ‘Derivation of the inductance’. Here, we derive the governing equations and provide additional details on the fitting procedure used to determine R, as presented in the main text.

The total number of atoms in each reservoir is measured directly using absorption images of both hyperfine states (|1⟩ and |3⟩), taken in rapid succession. To determine the total number of pairs in each reservoir Nl,r, we use both measurements, as this reduces statistical uncertainty. Specifically, \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}}}=({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|1\rangle }+{N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|3\rangle })/2\), where \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|i\rangle }\) denotes the number of atoms in the left and right reservoirs in state |i⟩. However, the second image (state |3⟩) highlights a cloud that has absorbed some energy from the first imaging pulse and is therefore slightly distorted. To avoid systematic effects from this distortion on C and T, we use only the image of the lowest hyperfine state (|1⟩) to extract the compressibility and temperature of the cloud, assuming these are identical for both states. We verified that our preparation is equivalent for both states by inverting the imaging sequence. We describe our system in terms of pairs and report C, L and R for pairs and pair currents, respectively.

Sources indicate that as shown in Fig. 2b, our RLC circuit consists of two capacitors (reservoirs) in series. We replace these two capacitors C by an effective capacitance Ceff = C/2. With this replacement, we obtain a standard RLC series circuit with an initially charged capacitor but no externally applied voltage.

Applying Kirchhoff’s voltage law and charge conservation, we find.

Using the mapping Q ↔ ΔN/2 and Ceff = C/2, we obtain.

It has been revealed that phase slips and vortices induce nonlinear resistances, so R = R(I) or R = R(J), where I and J denote the pair current and pair-current density, respectively. Depending on the model, we use.

Equations (9) and (10) are then integrated numerically.

Industry observers note that experimentally, transport is initiated by ramping down a blue-detuned beam that blocks the channel. A sudden quench of this beam slightly perturbs the reservoirs, so we instead ramp it down over 10 ms. This introduces an unknown initial condition I(t = 0). For each curve, we fit I(t = 0) ∈ [0, Iavg], where Iavg is the average current during the initial decay (before oscillations). To avoid giving undue weight to the first measured point, we fit ΔNfit(t = 0) ∈ [0.8, 1.2] ⋅ ΔNmeasured(t = 0). These bounds are necessary to prevent the models from ignoring the initial decay outside their validity regime. In particular, this is the case for the LAMH model when fitting data of wide channels, where only a few points represent the initial dynamics.

For numerical stability, R0 and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) are fitted on a logarithmic scale, whereas α and w0 are fitted linearly.

Industry observers note that finally, we discuss the fitting weights. Each configuration (t, w) has five measurements. Points with preparation errors (low atom number) are excluded, typically leaving four to five measurements per point and occasionally three. The experimental standard deviation is calculated for each configuration individually. We assume that for a given w, the uncertainty is independent of t. To prevent the fit from being dominated by points with unrealistically small uncertainties, both the fitting and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) calculations replace individual error bars with the median error bar of all the data sharing w.

According to recent reports, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis shown in Fig. 2c is performed as follows. The uncertainty of the measured points is assumed to be identical for all points belonging to a specific channel width. For each channel width, the model is fitted, either with 2.5 effective degrees of freedom (R0, w0, ΔN0, I0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0},\alpha ,\Delta {N}_{0},{I}_{0}\)), where the first two parameters are shared among four channels (2/4 = 0.5) if the channel participates in the global fit of the respective model, or two degrees of freedom (ΔN0, I0) otherwise. The reduced chi-squared is then calculated using \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}=\frac{1}{n-m}\sum \frac{{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}}{{\sigma }^{2}}\), where mi are the measured values, fi the corresponding values fitted by the model, σ the uncertainty shared by all measurement points of a specific width, n the number of measured points and m = 2.5 or m = 2 the number of effectively fitted degrees of freedom.

We discuss how the fitted models are affected by the various sources of systematic uncertainty. Specifically, we investigate how systematic uncertainties in the capacitance C, the channel width w and the temperature T affect the quality of the model fits and the inferred parameters RLAMH and α.

Assume that the true physical capacitance \(\widetilde{C}\) differs from the calculated value (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) by a factor γ, such that \(C=\gamma \widetilde{C}\). In our analysis, the effective inductance L is determined (see section ‘Derivation of the inductance’) before fitting the resistance by analysing the underdamped, multi-period oscillations of the system. Owing to the observation of multiple periods, the frequency can be measured with good accuracy and precision. A systematic shift γ ≠ 1 would therefore result in an inverse scaling of the extracted inductance curve, \(L\approx \widetilde{L}/\gamma \), where \(\widetilde{L}\) represents the true physical inductance. Inspecting the underlying equation of motion of the circuit (equation (2)) demonstrates that the extracted resistance scales identically with this factor (R ∝ 1/γ). This uniform rescaling by 1/α can be absorbed in the prefactor R0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\), leaving the quality of the fits, scalings, the inferred dynamic ranges and the geometric suppression constant w0 entirely unaffected.

The geometric potential landscape is projected onto the atoms using a DMD. Although physical pixel spacing and optical demagnification ratio are known accurately, the primary source of spatial uncertainty stems from the finite resolution of the imaging optics. The finite resolution effectively blurs the repulsive potential walls of the channel. Consequently, having to choose where to define the sharp boundaries of the model (spaced by w) within this blurred profile introduces a systematic uncertainty Δw.

Importantly, this geometric uncertainty of roughly 0.5 μm is expected to be shared across all channel configurations and does not affect each channel independently of the others. For channels in the 1D regime, the initial discharge through the narrowest channels is characterized by an extended period of nearly constant current in which inertial forces are negligible (∣L dI/dt∣ ≪ |RI|). In this regime, the system behaves predominantly as a nonlinear RC circuit, approximately decoupling the resistance fit from the precise value of L. Then, a uniform translation of w by Δw alters the resistances by a constant factor. For the LAMH model, \(R(w+\Delta w)\propto \exp (-\Delta w/{w}_{0})\). Similarly to the capacitance error, this effect is entirely absorbed by a re-normalization of the global prefactor R0, preserving both the dynamic range of RLAMH and its slope set by w0. The relatively high value of \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) for the LAMH model might be caused by the experiment that violates the assumption of box-like channel potentials. For the channels in the 2D regime, Δw/w ≪ 1, so we expect systematic effects caused by Δw ≠ 0 to be small and the approximation of modelling the channels as box-like to be safe.

Industry observers note that although we calibrated our measurements with the thermodynamic reference point of Bose–Einstein condensation, our measured atom-pair numbers and temperatures (see sections ‘High-saturation imaging’ and ‘Thermodynamic state extraction by 2D equation of state fitting’) might be subject to systematic errors. An error in the inferred pair-number \(N=\gamma \widetilde{N}\), where N is the inferred particle number and \(\widetilde{N}\) is the physical particle number, would force a corresponding shift in C, thereby rescaling L and R as discussed above. Moreover, it would rescale I. As the current enters the expression for the resistance in the vortex model only in the form of a power law, it would merely shift \(\widetilde{R}\) by a constant factor γ−α. Again, this constant factor would affect neither α, nor the quality of the vortex-model fits, nor the quality of its scaling law. As the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, it is unaffected by potential systematic effects in T. For the LAMH model, the situation is different. The temperature enters the model explicitly through I0 = 2kBT/h. Variations in both N and T ultimately tie into the ratio I/I0. Because this ratio controls the degree of nonlinearity of the circuit, we can model their combined systematic impact by analysing variations in I0 alone.

According to recent reports, the initial discharge of the narrowest channels is distinctly nonlinear (implying I ≫ I0), whereas the subsequent oscillations are approximately sinusoidal (implying I ≱ I0). Consequently, the ratio I/I0 is constrained by the geometric profile of the relaxation curves. However, systematic effects that affect the ratio I/I0 do also affect the quality of fit and the dynamic range of RLAMH. In general, if I/I0 is lowered (by decreasing I or increasing T), the circuit is less nonlinear and the dynamic range of RLAMH decreases, whereas an increase in the ratio has the opposite effect. Although the parameter I0 is constrained in the LAMH model, we performed additional fittings, where I0 was a global fit parameter, to effectively account for potential systematic errors in I or T. The best fits are achieved with I0,fit = 3.50(1)I0, reducing \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) averaged over the five narrowest channels, by more than a factor of 2. A possible cause for this could be that the attractive Gaussian beam illuminating the channel locally heats the channel, thereby increasing I0. Note that this beam also increases the local degeneracy such that we would still expect the channel to be deeply degenerate. Although in the case of fitted I0, the dynamic range of RLAMH is reduced, it continues to span more than four orders of magnitude. The values are still in good agreement with the predicted exponential scaling.

Recent findings suggest that for all channel widths except the narrowest one, we observe underdamped, long-lived oscillations. As these oscillations remain underdamped, the influence of the nonlinear resistance on the oscillation frequency is expected to be small. To extract the inductance of the channel for each width (except the narrowest one), we exclude the initial transient dynamics up to the first, global minimum occurring at a time t = t1,w. The remaining data are fitted with a damped sinusoidal function \({f}_{w}(t)={A}_{w}\exp (-(t-{t}_{1,w})/{\tau }_{w})\sin ({\omega }_{w}t+{\phi }_{{\rm{w}}})+\Delta {N}_{w,\mathrm{offset}},\) where Aw, τw, ωw, ϕw, and ΔNw,offset are fitting parameters. Small offsets |ΔNw,offset| < 0.018 account for potential alignment errors that cause the oscillations to centre around slightly nonzero values. Using the inferred effective capacitance Ceff of our circuit (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’), we determine the total inductance for a given channel width as \({L}_{w}=1/(({\omega }_{w}^{2}+{\tau }_{w}^{-2}){C}_{\mathrm{eff}})\approx 1/({\omega }_{w}^{2}C),\) where the approximation is equivalent to the result for an undamped LC circuit and holds for weakly damped circuits. Although the quantitative difference in our case is minute, we do include the τ-term capturing the effect of the resistance lowering the oscillation frequency of the RLC circuit. Note that for the wide channels in particular, fitting a damped sine to the oscillatory data is a pragmatic choice that allows for an approximation of the inductance, the signature of which is primarily contained in the frequency of the oscillation. Over extended periods of time, however, the damped sine and the dynamics of the vortex model would appear different, as the latter does not feature an exponentially decaying amplitude. This kinetic inductance Lw quantifies the kinetic energy associated with a given pair current I. Although the main contribution arises from the transport channel itself, there is also a residual contribution because of particle motion in the adjoining 2D and 3D regions, whose geometries are independent of the channel width. We therefore write \(L(w)={L}_{\mathrm{channel}}(w)+{L}_{\mathrm{res}}\). Assuming a constant particle density inside the channel, the mass of particles in the transport channel (M) scales with its width, M ∝ w. For a given current, the corresponding particle velocity in the channel thus scales inversely, \({v}_{\mathrm{channel}}\propto \frac{1}{w}\). Consequently, the kinetic energy associated with a fixed I scales as \({E}_{\mathrm{kin}}=M{v}_{\mathrm{channel}}^{2}/2\propto w{(1/w)}^{2}=1/w\), implying that Lchannel(w) ∝ 1/w. We therefore model the total inductance as.

Industry observers note that with fitting parameters ℓc and Lres. We find ℓc/h = 3.01(3) × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06(4) × 10−6 s, where the uncertainties represent the standard errors of the fit. The measured inductances Lw and the fitted model are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. The excellent agreement of the model with the data validates our model assumptions.

In a previous, comparable experimental setting, we estimated the atoms traversing a region of length d ≈ 3 μm in a time t ≈ 330 μs, resulting in an estimated atomic velocity of v ≈ 9 mm s−1 (ref. 48). As our channel is practically defect free, we assume that the atomic velocity is close to the critical velocity vc. So we estimate 4ξ ≈ 4ħ/(mvc) ≈ 5 μm (ref. 49).

In a recent development, given the method with which we extract the energy ratio, two main sources of error are to be considered. The first one is the statistical noise of the measurement points. This directly translates into an uncertainty of the inferred energy ratio but also causes a systematic bias towards higher values, as only the extrema of the signals are considered. The second contribution comes from the finite sampling rate of the oscillations. This causes an uncertainty and a bias towards lower values, as the measured points do not sample the peaks exactly. To quantitatively assess their influence for all our measurements, we performed Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, we sampled sinusoidal signals with the frequencies, amplitudes and dampings observed in the signals used for Fig. 4. We sampled these artificial signals with the sampling rates and statistical noise that occurred in the physical experiment. This simulation yielded the following insight: For the data presented in Fig. 4, the inferred energies have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a standard deviation smaller than 2%.

Although several studies have reported on Josephson oscillations with seemingly similar measurements in comparable settings27,28,29, our system operates far outside the Josephson regime. The Josephson effect requires the junction length to be much shorter than the superconducting coherence length, which for our system is close to the healing length4,12. In our case, the channel length ℓ = 27 μm is much larger than the estimated healing length ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’). Moreover, we observe neither a well-defined current-phase relation nor an oscillation amplitude consistent with the Josephson relation. The former statement is based on time-of-flight measurements of the relative phase of the two reservoirs with the same preparation performed in a slightly different geometry. Although for the data shown in this manuscript, we always observe the same initial dynamics (up to small noise), these additional measurements confirm that the prepared phase between the two reservoirs is not controlled, sampling values between 0 and 2π from a flat distribution. We therefore conclude that the oscillatory signal observed in our experiment cannot be attributed to JO.

Extended Data Fig. 2 provides additional data related to Fig. 3. The theoretical motivation and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis presented in Fig. 2 already justify the choice of models. The data shown here complements that analysis by demonstrating that the scaling laws reported in Fig. 3 are not numerical artefacts and are not imposed by the fitting procedure.

For both the LAMH and vortex models, the predicted scalings break down outside their respective ranges of validity. This behaviour indicates that the observed scaling is not a numerical consequence of the fitting procedure and is not artificially enforced by the functional form of the models.

Industry observers note that the saturation of the LAMH-inferred resistance at large widths does not seem to be due to limited fitting precision, fitting boundaries or lack of convergence. Instead, it reflects a transition from the strong exponential width dependence characteristic of the LAMH model to a much weaker dependence, as predicted by the vortex model.

For the vortex model, the trend reverses in the crossover regime, showing a clear deviation from the scaling expected by that model.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One of football’s largest financial lenders abandoned a planned £1.5billion loan to Manchester City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.
  • The decision by US private capital group Apollo Global Management is the latest evidence that the money markets deem City a financial risk, as the club prepare an appeal against their conviction on the vast majority of 115 Premier League charges of inflating income through sham contracts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 11:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 11:59 EST, 19 November 2026.

One of football’s largest financial lenders abandoned a planned £1.5billion loan to Manchester City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

The decision by US private capital group Apollo Global Management is the latest evidence that the money markets deem City a financial risk, as the club prepare an appeal against their conviction on the vast majority of 115 Premier League charges of inflating income through sham contracts.

It was reported by Bloomberg last week that a German lender, Oldenburgische Landesbank (OL), had pulled out of a deal that would have let Brazilian top-flight side Palmeiras take a large upfront payment against instalments City are due to pay them for midfielder Allan Elias, signed this summer for £32million with £2m add-ons. That bank views City as a reputational and financial risk.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Apollo was in the final stages of negotiating the loan to City Football Group (CFG) in September, when the deal collapsed after the ruling that they artificially inflated their financial position to the tune of more than £900m over nine years.

According to recent reports, city owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan injected £100m into the club in the month after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Mansour, who has only been present at one City home game since Abu Dhabi bought the club in 2008, has made no public comment on the club’s conviction, which delivers huge reputational damage to his image-conscious country.

There are signs that football is preparing for a strong legal attack from Abu Dhabi if City lose their appeal. Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors in the event of sponsors Etihad and Etisalat suing them, it was also revealed on Thursday. Legal indemnity will be in place for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittain and three other non-executive directors.

US private capital group Apollo Global Management abandoned a £1.5billion loan to Man City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

City owner Sheikh Mansou injected £100m into the club after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi.

But the refusal of credit by Apollo, which has loaned £80m to Premier League football club Nottingham Forest and has a minority stake in Championship side Wrexham, demonstrates that the capital markets think City are imperilled, with the appeal process by no means straightforward.

It has been revealed that if an appeal failed, City could seek a judicial review of the commission's findings at the High Court. But to do so, they would need to demonstrate that the Premier League acted outside its powers or reached a conclusion which no reasonable authority could have reached. City would need the High Court’s permission to make a judicial review application and the bar is high.

Financial analyst Paul Quinn wrote on The Esk website that Apollo’s issue had been with City, not Abu Dhabi itself. Three weeks ago, Apollo agreed to take a minority stake in Mubadala Capital, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund chaired by Sheikh Mansour and run by City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak. Apollo and City have not commented.

Quinn said that CFG needed the money because it was not self-funding, despite City’s financial strength. CFG’s pre-tax loss widened from £122.2m to £292.3m in the last financial year. City produced £694.1m of CFG’s £888m group revenue and ran up a £9m loss.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The former Brighton star sat out of games against Tottenham, Manchester United, Sunderland and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup with the Blues losing three of those four in his absence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joao Pedro has been ruled out of Chelsea’s Premier League clash with Leeds United this weekend.

The Brazil international has missed his side’s last four games as a result of a thigh injury he suffered in training in October.

The former Brighton star sat out of games against Tottenham, Manchester United, Sunderland and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup with the Blues losing three of those four in his absence.

There was hope he would be available to return after the international break but Xabi Alonso has confirmed his striker is still not ready ahead of the visit of Daniel Farke’s side on Saturday afternoon.

Pedro is still to return to training with his manager unable to put a timeline on his return.

It has been revealed that ‘Not yet,’ Alonso remarked when asked about his availability. ‘He’s not fit yet to train with the team. He’s not going to be available for Leeds. We need to see game by game how he’s feeling.’.

When asked how confident he is to find a solution in attack in Pedro’s absence, Alonso replied: ’We need the whole team for that.

’It’s not just the strikers who can score. We can score from set-pieces, defenders, midfielders, so it’s teamwork, for sure.’He’s an important player but we need to deal this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.’They [Danny Welbeck and Emmanuel Emegha] are both ready, both have different qualities, both at different stages of their career. Danny has played so many games, has great experience, has quality, Emman has this power, this physicality, he’s waiting for his chance and we have enough games to try.’.

Chelsea have other concerns with Maxence Lacroix still sidelined along with Jorrel Hato.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Lacroix, almost ever-present at the back since his summer arrival from Crystal Palace, came off with a hamstring injury in the Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool while Hato missing the last three games with a back concern.

‘He’s [Lacroix] not fit to play tomorrow and he’s a similar situation with Joao,’ Alonso said.

Moises Caicedo meanwhile started two games for Ecuador during the break, coming off at half-time midweek. Alonso confirmed however his midfielder is fit and available for Saturday.

Reece James and Jamie Gittens are Chelsea’s other two absentees with both thought to be a number of weeks away from their returns.

Your weekly briefing on Tottenham, featuring team news and expert analysis from Sam Tabuteau.

Recent findings suggest that I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice.

Luca Williams-Barnett starts for Tottenham against Ipswich today.

Destiny Udogie, Savio, James Maddison and Lucas Bergvall were all pictured training at Hotspur Way this week and are now in contention for minutes on Saturday.

Udogie was left out of Roberto De Zerbi’s squad as Spurs lost 1-0 to Leeds before the international break, though the Italian left-back took to social media to suggest that he was not injured.

De Zerbi had previously mentioned that Udogie’s injuries were becoming “problematic”, with the 23-year-old starting just two league games this season. He has slotted back into the starting lineup this afternoon.

It has been revealed that savio, meanwhile, is in line to return to action for the first time since October’s 1-1 draw with Manchester United. The Brazilian winger has missed Tottenham’s last four league games with a muscular problem and is on the bench.

Spurs sorely lacked a creative threat against Leeds. But despite naming Maddison on the bench at Elland Road, De Zerbi didn't bring him on in search of a goal, raising concerns about his fitness.

Maddison has struggled to train consistently since the start of the season and came off midway through Spurs’ 2-0 win over Chelsea with a suspected groin problem.

The 29-year-old has not featured since that historic victory at Stamford Bridge, despite being available for selection. After working on his fitness throughout the international break, he returns to the starting lineup here.

Mathys Tel is expected to be out for up to three weeks with an Achilles injury sustained following a heavy tackle from Leeds defender Jayden Bogle.

There is a fresh injury concern for De Zerbi, though, as Sandro Tonali has missed out on the matchday squad altogether, with the reason for his absence presently unconfirmed.

Tottenham XI vs Ipswich: Kinsky, Porro, Van Hecke, Senesi, Udogie, Fernandes, Gallagher, Kudus, Williams-Barnett, Maddison, Solanke.

Subs: Dubravka, Robertson, Van de Ven, Gray, Bergvall, Savio, Kulusevski, Bentancur, Marmoush.

Injured: Simons, Odobert, Tel, Mudryk, Tosin.

Time and date: 3pm GMT on Saturday November 21, 2026.

Venue: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 20 Nov 2026 21:40, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 21:42.

Konyaspor will be looking to halt their recent slide down the Turkish Super Lig standings when they welcome Besiktas to Medas Konya Buyuksehir Stadyumu on Sunday afternoon.

The hosts sit 15th in the table with eight points from 11 matches, only outside the bottom three on goal difference, while the Black Eagles occupy fifth place with 19 points from 10 games and will be hoping to maintain their push towards the top of the standings.

Konyaspor have endured a difficult run of results in recent weeks, winning just once in their last six league matches and struggling to find consistency in the final third.

Ilhan Palut's side began that sequence with consecutive goalless draws against Kasimpasa and Istanbul Basaksehir before suffering a 1-0 defeat away to Amed SK.

They then recorded a 2-0 home victory over Genclerbirligi, but that proved to be their only success during the period as they suffered consecutive defeats against Galatasaray (4-0) and Samsunspor (1-0).

Konyaspor were particularly disappointing in their defeat away to Samsunspor just before the break, failing to take anything from a match against a side sitting second-bottom and enduring a losing run.

The result further highlighted their struggles in front of goal, with the hosts having scored just six times in their opening 11 league matches, an average of fewer than one per game, while they have failed to find the net in seven of those fixtures.

Konyaspor have scored four of their six goals and collected seven of their eight points on home soil, although they were thrashed by Galatasaray in their last home game and now face a Besiktas side that have beaten them in their last two league meetings.

The hosts did manage to defeat the Black Eagles 1-0 in their most recent encounter, although that victory came in the Turkish Cup.

Besiktas, meanwhile, have enjoyed a more productive campaign, collecting seven wins, one draw and three defeats from their opening 11 league matches to remain within reach of the leading teams, sitting six points behind league leaders Galatasaray.

Vincenzo Italiano's side are also unbeaten in their last three league games, a sequence that began with a 2-0 home victory over Istanbul Basaksehir before they were held to a 2-2 draw by Kasimpasa.

Their subsequent European fixture saw them suffer a 3-2 defeat against Celtic, but they responded positively three days later by recording a convincing 3-0 home win over Genclerbirligi.

Dusan Vlahovic was particularly influential in that victory, scoring twice as the Black Eagles returned to winning ways in the Super Lig and demonstrated the attacking quality that has made them one of the more productive sides in the division, with only four teams scoring more than their 23 goals.

However, the visitors have struggled on the road, winning just one of their five away league matches and failing to win any of their last three, during which they have recorded one draw and two defeats.

Konyaspor will be without Adil Demirbag, who is recovering from a cruciate ligament injury and is expected to remain sidelined for the rest of the season.

Chidozie Awaziem is also unlikely to feature after sustaining a muscle injury, while Marko Jevtovic is working towards regaining full fitness and faces a late assessment.

Ugurcan Yazgili is another concern after picking up a hamstring problem, leaving Palut with defensive and midfield decisions to make.

Mostafa Mohamed, Diogo Goncalves and Ebrima Colley are among the attacking options available to the Konyaspor manager, although Enis Bardhi is expected to miss out through suspension.

Besiktas will be without Umit Akdag, who is recovering from a broken wrist, while Fabio Miretti is also expected to miss the match with a shoulder injury.

Emmanuel Agbadou is not expected to return until later in December as he continues his recovery from a knee problem, while Orkun Kokcu is also sidelined with a foot injury.

Konyaspor possible starting lineup:.

Gungordu; Andzouana, Baniya, Bosluk, Masuaku; Toth, Ibrahimoglu; Colley, Goncalves, Dompe; Mohamed.

Besiktas possible starting lineup:.

Nubel; Murillo, Taylan Bulut, Topcu, R Yilmaz; Ndidi; Trossard, S Ozcan, Olaitan, Fakili; Vlahovic.

Konyaspor have struggled to produce consistent attacking performances this season, and although Besiktas have been inconsistent on the road, their attacking quality should be enough to overcome the hosts' defensive resistance, with Italiano's side expected to secure a comfortable victory in Konya.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For much of this sticky night in Naples, Arsenal appeared to be starting the fresh Champions League campaign the same way they finished the last one: by erroneously smashing the ball into the stands behind the goal.

Memories of Gabriel Magalhães’s ballooned penalty in the final against Paris St-Germain remain fresh in the mind, and here his team-mates were lining up to produce their own versions. Bukayo Saka and Piero Hincapié, especially, delivered astonishing misses which were closer to entering orbit than the opposition net.

According to recent reports, thankfully for Arsenal, though, there was one player who was in no mood to relive the frustration of that shoot-out loss 14 weeks ago. Martin Odegaard has started this season in truly fabulous form and here he scored a truly fabulous late goal, fizzed into the corner from range, to cap another inventive individual performance and earn three points for his team.

Great play 😮‍💨Martin Ødegaard rounds off a wonderful passing move for Arsenal 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FrH6gW8Ak4.

In a recent development, in five matches this season, Odegaard has already scored four goals. That is three more than he managed in the whole of last season. The Arsenal captain is fit again and he is flowing. As ever, when Odegaard flows, Arsenal flow.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s what we need, the players with that mindset to decide the game and play with that personality,” said Mikel Arteta. “He has got that edge. He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games.”.

In the end it was a thoroughly deserved victory for the Premier League side, who were superior to Napoli in every department. Were it not for their comically bad finishing, they would have guaranteed the result long before Odegaard’s 75th-minute strike.

Industry observers note that their expected goals figure suggested they should have scored more than four goals, compared to Napoli’s 0.22. In total, they registered 26 shots – the most of any Arsenal team on record in a single Champions League match, and the most on record a Napoli team has ever faced.

“With the amount of chances we generated, the scoreline has to reflect a very different result,” said Arteta. “The number of players that got into this situation, the amount of situations that we generated in various ways was something that pleased me a lot.”.

There was, almost inevitably, another clean sheet for Arteta’s side. They had the best defence in the Champions League last season, conceding only seven goals in 15 matches, and they were largely untroubled here. Ezri Konsa was once again excellent, in only his second start for the club. He successfully wrapped up Rasmus Hojlund, the former Manchester United centre-forward, and was as calm in possession as the absent William Saliba would have been. A potential injury to right-back Ben White was a concern, though.

The Champions League is the one that Arsenal have never won and, you suspect, the one that Arteta really wants. Success in this competition would elevate Arsenal to a higher level as a club and fully establish Arteta as one of the great coaching minds of his generation.

According to recent reports, to lose last season’s final in such painful circumstances clearly hurt the Arsenal manager, who was visibly distraught after that shoot-out defeat despite the obvious delight of winning the Premier League title. If you could give him the choice between retaining the league this season or leading Arsenal to their first European Cup, he would surely pick the latter.

Arsenal have now won THIRTEEN UCL League Phase games in a row 🔴🔥 pic.twitter.com/UmcfMYO13r.

Sources indicate that A trip to Naples in the first round of the league phase made for a lovely opening tie: atmospheric, intense and competitive. Napoli have had a difficult start to their campaign, losing two of three Serie A games so far, but they possess real quality and have a top manager in Massimiliano Allegri.

Recent findings suggest that even at the age of 35, the great Kevin De Bruyne still has power in his boots and schemes in his mind. When he tested Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya from range in the first half, it would have triggered horrible flashbacks in the minds of the travelling supporters. In his previous 17 starts against Arsenal for Manchester City, De Bruyne had scored eight goals and registered four assists. Thankfully for Arsenal, it was the only moment in which De Bruyne really threatened.

Throughout this game, Arsenal moved the ball around with precision and purpose. They created an extraordinary amount of chances, with Saka and Hincapié missing the best of them. Saka’s effort in the first half, when one-v-one with the goalkeeper, was strangely erratic. Hincapié’s opportunity, meanwhile, was laughable. Two yards out from goal, he somehow put the ball onto the running track that surrounds the pitch at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

Recent findings suggest that despite all the wasted chances, Arsenal kept going. Odegaard, in particular, kept probing. His goal was gorgeous: a swift exchange of passes between him, White and Christos Tzolis resulted in the Arsenal captain firing his effort from the edge of the area. Delicate build-up, ferocious finish.

In keeping with the theme of the night, Arsenal should have scored more. Noni Madueke, for example, missed a one-v-one when it seemed like he had all the time in the world. But Odegaard’s intervention eventually proved to be enough, as he once again stood forward as Arsenal’s match-winner.

That’s all from us, but we’ll be back tomorrow night to bring you Man Utd’s return to the Champions League against Sabah!

"I think the chemistry, especially in the front players, has been exceptional." ✨Mikel Arteta tells @AnitaNnekaJones how impressed he's been by the connection between Martin Ødegaard and Christos Tzolis 🤝 pic.twitter.com/J6VOAMk4Lm.

Arsenal extend their #UCL unbeaten streak 👏 pic.twitter.com/wFBga6lNrN.

"We missed so many big chances"Mikel Arteta shares his thoughts after Arsenal's victory over Napoli 💭🎙️ @DannyJamieson | 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/zT2bHcPoiH.

Before all of that, Arsenal will now have to turn their attention to the Stadium of Light as they travel to Sunderland on Saturday.

They then face Ipswich Town in the EFL Cup on Tuesday night, before travelling to Brighton on the weekend.

It has been revealed that “Everything runs through Martin Odegaard,” remarked Cole on TNT Sports. “He can stand still and find space. He is at the peak of his powers and it is beautiful to watch.

“You can’t help but love watching him play his football.”.

Plenty of praise for Martin Odegaard on TNT, with former Arsenal man Martin Keown heralding the captain’s behaviour.

It has been revealed that “He’s setting an example to his players. He’s fitter, he’s hungry, and he did his talking on the pitch. He came good for his team.”.

Couple that with his impressive chemistry with fresh arrival Christos Tzolis, and there is a lot of goal-scoring potential there this season. Three of the winger’s four assists have been for his captain, and we’re barely a month into the season.

“We know what this competition means to all of us, the experience of last year as well, so we need to start with the first game in a really, really tough place, but really excited to start the campaign.

Louis Saha believes Manchester United should have signed Nicolas Jackson before his £65million move from Chelsea to Aston Villa.

Jackson enjoyed a fast start to life at Chelsea, scoring 17 goals in all competitions during his first season at Stamford Bridge.

But the Senegalese striker failed to hit those heights during the 2024-25 campaign and Chelsea sent him on loan to Bayern Munich last season.

The performances of Joao Pedro complicated Jackson’s future upon his return from his loan in Germany, and a sale to Villa was eventually sanctioned, reuniting the 25-year-old with his former Villarreal boss Unai Emery.

Back under Emery’s tutelage, Jackson has returned to his best, with nine goals in 14 appearances so far this season.

And Saha believes United missed a trick by not trying to sign Jackson over the summer, particularly given Benjamin Sesko’s injury woes, which have seen him miss large swathes of this campaign.

‘Nicolas Jackson is a player that I think Man Utd really missed out on because he’s an experienced striker who plays well under pressure,’ Saha told CasinoHawks.

‘Of course, he misses chances sometimes, but his work rate and ability to keep opposing centre-backs busy are vital for team balance.

‘Aston Villa have done really well with those two players, I would’ve loved them at Old Trafford.’.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has insisted he was not involved ‘in any wrongdoings’ during his time at Manchester City amid the ongoing case against his former employers.

An independent commission found City guilty of breaching more than 100 of the Premier League’s financial rules in September between the period of 2009 and 2018.

City have appealed against the ruling and repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

Berrada joined United in January 2024 having spent over a decade working in various roles for City Football Group.

He was named the club’s CEO in 2016 and remained in that role until 2020 when he was named City Football Group’s chief football operations officer for the next four years.

Recent findings suggest that berrada’s time at the club’s CEO overlaps with the period in which City were investigated. But the United chief has no concerns over any implications for him in the case.

‘I’m not concerned,’ Berrada told Sky Sports.

‘I want to be very clear about this: I wasn’t involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn’t involved in the proceedings. There are no allegations against me.

‘In that sense, there will be no surprises.’.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Asked whether United could look to pursue compensation if City fail in their appeal, Berrada replied: ‘I don’t want to comment on that because right now, it’s an ongoing process.

‘When it runs its course, then we’ll take a view on what is our position as Manchester United.’.

Berrada and the rest of United’s hierarchy have just presided over their third mid-season managerial sacking in three years with Mauricio Pochettino the latest to be tasked with lifting the club from its malaise.

‘If you think about the fact that we’ve had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven’t achieved the stability that we want to – that’s for sure,’ Berrada mentioned.

‘There are different circumstances as to why it didn’t work out with Erik, Ruben and now Michael. And we’re always learning. We’re always trying to improve and understand what has failed.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 20 Nov 2026 22:07.

Trabzonspor will look to extend their winning run in the league to seven games when they host bottom-placed Eyupspor at Papara Park on Sunday.

The Black Sea outfit sit second in the Turkish Super Lig standings with 25 points from 11 matches, three behind league leaders Galatasaray, while the visitors are 18th with just three points, five adrift of safety.

Thomas Reis has made an excellent start to his reign, winning all six of his league games in charge, with the latest victory coming in a 2-0 away triumph over Alanyaspor just before the international break, as Wagner Pina opened the scoring in the 17th minute before Muhammed Salah doubled their advantage in the 34th.

That result represented a strong response to their 1-0 defeat to Freiburg in the Conference League, which brought an end to their seven-game winning streak across all competitions.

Trabzonspor will now look to begin another run of victories, and their attacking and defensive records suggest they have every reason to be confident, having scored 26 goals, the fourth-highest tally in the division, while conceding just eight, the fewest in the league, as they build a strong foundation in their pursuit of a first league title since 2021-22.

The hosts have also won all five of their league games at home this season, and another victory would see them match the club's best start to a home league campaign, last achieved in 1984-85.

Meanwhile, Eyupspor are in deep trouble after suffering a 2-0 defeat to Kocaelispor last time out, their eighth consecutive league loss and the ninth time in 11 matches this season that they have failed to score in the division.

No other side has conceded more goals than Eyupspor this season, with their tally standing at 30, while they have also scored just three times, the fewest in the league.

Mustafa Dalci remarked after the defeat to Kocaelispor that his side are entering a period in which they must start collecting points, but their prospects look bleak ahead of another difficult away fixture, particularly as they have conceded a league-high 19 goals on their travels.

Their head-to-head record against Trabzonspor offers little encouragement either, with Eyupspor yet to win any of their four previous meetings, drawing one and losing three, while they have failed to score in all four encounters.

Reis has several absentees to contend with, including defender Chibuike Nwaiwu, who is suspended after accumulating yellow cards.

Batagov, Franculino Dju, Ruslan Malinovskyi and Okay Yokuslu are also expected to miss out, although a number of injured players have returned to training, with Ernest Muci, Tim Jabol-Folcarelli and Wagner Pina all potentially available after recovering from their respective problems.

Aral Simsir is also being assessed ahead of the match, while Cihan Canak and Onuralp Cevikkan remain injury concerns, leaving Reis with several selection decisions to make before naming his squad.

Eyupspor, meanwhile, have their own injury problems, with Talha Ulvan, Omer Ceyhan, Ahmed Abdullahi, Bilal Boutobba, Lenny Pintor and Simone Giordano all listed as unavailable or doubtful.

Dalci could therefore be forced to make changes, particularly in defence and attack, although the visitors are expected to retain much of the starting XI that faced Kocaelispor before the international break.

Trabzonspor possible starting lineup:.

Onana; Pina, Savic, Cenk Ozkacar, Cabral; Fabinho, Tufan; Salah, Muci, Saviolo; Onuachu.

Eyupspor possible starting lineup:.

Moldovan; Yavuz, El Yamiq, Jules, Yasar; Massanga, Akman; Michalak, Sabiri, Yao; Abdullahi.

Trabzonspor have the league's best defensive record, an impressive winning run, home advantage and a dominant head-to-head record against Eyupspor, all of which point towards a comfortable victory for the hosts, who should also be capable of keeping a clean sheet against the division's lowest-scoring side.
